questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A preparer relies on a carryover figure taken from a previously filed return. What must be confirmed?
options: That the client's copy matches the original as filed
That the position relied upon has not been adjusted by examination or otherwise
That the earlier preparer held a valid PTIN
Nothing; reliance on a filed return is unqualified
questions.pageTitle: Use of prior years' returns for comparison, accuracy and carryovers

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: How long may an individual carry forward an unused excess charitable contribution?
options: Indefinitely
Three succeeding years
Five succeeding years, in order of time
Twenty succeeding years
questions.explanation: An amount not used by the fifth succeeding year expires.
questions.pageTitle: Use of prior years' returns for comparison, accuracy and carryovers

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: What happens to the character of a capital loss carried forward?
options: All carryovers become short-term
All carryovers become long-term
Short-term and long-term components carry forward separately and retain their character
Character is redetermined each year by the taxpayer
questions.pageTitle: Use of prior years' returns for comparison, accuracy and carryovers

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A taxpayer has net operating losses from 2016 and from 2021. How is the deduction computed?
options: The combined amount, limited to 80 percent of taxable income
The 2016 loss in full first, with the 80 percent limitation applied only to the 2021 layer
The 2021 loss first, because later losses take priority
Each layer limited to 80 percent separately
questions.explanation: Pre-2018 losses are allowed in full and are absorbed first.
questions.pageTitle: Use of prior years' returns for comparison, accuracy and carryovers

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A disallowed passive activity loss is carried forward. How is it treated?
options: As a deduction against any income in the next year
As a capital loss in the next year
As a deduction or credit allocable to the same activity in the next taxable year
It expires after five years
questions.explanation: which is why suspended losses must be tracked activity by activity.
questions.pageTitle: Use of prior years' returns for comparison, accuracy and carryovers

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which is not a minimum requirement for filing a return?
options: Providing a social security card
The taxpayer's date of birth as an intake fact
The identifying number of each dependent claimed
The taxpayer's filing status
questions.explanation: The number must appear on the return; the physical card need not be produced and may be supplied verbally or in writing.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A taxpayer and both children hold ITINs. Which is available?
options: The child tax credit
The earned income credit
A dependency claim for each child
All of these
questions.explanation: An ITIN is a valid identifying number for filing and for claiming a dependent, but § 24(h)(7) and § 32(m) each require a social security number.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: What does IRC § 24(h)(7) require on the return as rewritten?
options: The qualifying child's social security number only
The taxpayer's social security number only
The taxpayer's social security number — or one spouse's on a joint return — and the child's
An ITIN for either the taxpayer or the child

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A qualifying child's social security number is issued two months after the return's due date. What is the effect on the earned income credit for that year?
options: The credit is allowed once the number is obtained
The credit is allowed if an extension was filed
The credit is not allowed for that taxable year
The credit is allowed at half the amount
questions.explanation: Section 32(m) requires the number to be issued on or before the due date for filing the return for the taxable year.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Publication 1345 says an ERO should ask a taxpayer not known to them for two forms of identification. What is the status of that guidance?
options: A statutory condition of filing a return
A preparer safeguard against identity theft refund fraud
A requirement only for paper returns
A condition of claiming any refundable credit
questions.explanation: It is addressed to the provider as a fraud safeguard, not to the taxpayer as a filing requirement.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which is not a means of ending lawful permanent resident status?
options: A voluntary written statement of intent to abandon, filed with the registration card
Failing the substantial presence test
Administrative termination by the immigration authority
A final judicial order of exclusion or deportation
questions.explanation: Resident status is deemed to continue unless rescinded or administratively or judicially determined to have been abandoned; the substantial presence test is a separate route into residency.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: An individual was present 90 days two years ago and 120 days last year. What is the minimum current-year presence that meets the substantial presence test?
questions.explanation: The prior years contribute 15 and 40, leaving 128 of the 183 required — and 128 also clears the separate 31-day condition.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which is not a requirement for obtaining an adoption taxpayer identification number?
options: The child is eligible to be claimed as a dependent
The child's SSN cannot be obtained from the birth parents despite reasonable attempts
A foreign adoption has a Permanent Resident Alien Card or Certificate of Citizenship
The adoption process has been completed
questions.explanation: The number exists for a pending adoption; completion is what ends it.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: An individual is present in the United States for 40 days in the current year and has a weighted three-year total of 200 days. What is the result?
options: Resident alien, because the weighted total exceeds 183
Resident alien, because presence exceeded 31 days
Nonresident alien, unless the closer connection exception is claimed
Resident alien only if a first-year election is made
questions.explanation: Both conditions are met — 40 days exceeds the 31-day minimum and the weighted total exceeds 183 — so the test is satisfied.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which of these does an ITIN do?
options: Authorise the holder to work in the United States
Qualify the holder for the earned income tax credit
Serve as identification outside the federal tax system
Provide a taxpayer identification number for federal tax purposes
questions.explanation: The IRS states that an ITIN does none of the other three.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Under the substantial presence test, which combination of facts, by itself, is sufficient to make a non-citizen a resident alien for the current year (absent an exception)?
options: Present in the U.S. for 20 days in the current year and 200 days in the prior year
Present in the U.S. for 40 days in the current year, with a weighted three-year total (current year plus one-third of the prior year plus one-sixth of the year before that) of at least 183 days
Present in the U.S. for any number of days in the current year, as long as the taxpayer holds a valid visa
Present in the U.S. for 100 days in the current year only, regardless of prior years
questions.explanation: The substantial presence test requires at least 31 days of presence in the current year AND a weighted total of at least 183 days across the current year (full weight), the prior year (one-third weight), and the year before that (one-sixth weight). A bare 20-day current-year count fails the 31-day threshold outright, no matter the weighted total.
questions.pageTitle: Residency status and/or citizenship (e.g., citizen, visas, green cards, resident alien or non-resident alien, ITIN)

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A taxpayer was a nonresident alien for part of the year and became a resident alien partway through the same year, with no election to be treated differently. What best describes this taxpayer's filing position for that year?
options: The taxpayer files only Form 1040-NR for the entire year
The taxpayer files only Form 1040 for the entire year, exactly as a full-year resident would

The taxpayer is a dual-status alien for the year, generally reporting the resident period and nonresident period under their respective rules, with restrictions such as not using the standard deduction for the dual-status return
The taxpayer chooses freely which single return to file for the whole year with no restrictions
questions.explanation: A taxpayer who is a nonresident alien for part of the year and a resident alien for the rest is a dual-status alien. The return reflects both periods, and dual-status filers face specific restrictions — for example, they generally cannot claim the standard deduction — that don't apply to a taxpayer who was a resident alien for the full year.
questions.pageTitle: Residency status and/or citizenship (e.g., citizen, visas, green cards, resident alien or non-resident alien, ITIN)

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: An individual is not eligible for a Social Security number but needs a U.S. taxpayer identification number to be listed on a return, for example as a nonresident alien spouse. What is true of the ITIN issued in this situation?
options: It authorizes the holder to work legally in the United States
It establishes eligibility for the earned income tax credit
It confers a particular immigration status on the holder
It is issued solely for federal tax reporting purposes and does none of the above
questions.explanation: An ITIN is issued strictly to allow federal tax reporting for people who need a taxpayer identification number but aren't eligible for a Social Security number. It does not authorize work, does not by itself establish eligibility for the earned income tax credit (which requires a valid SSN), and does not confer or change immigration status.
questions.pageTitle: Residency status and/or citizenship (e.g., citizen, visas, green cards, resident alien or non-resident alien, ITIN)

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: An individual dies on 1 May. The estate adopts a fiscal year ending 30 June. When is Form 1041 due, absent an extension?
options: 15 April
15 July
15 August
15 October
questions.explanation: A fiscal-year return is due the fifteenth day of the fourth month following the close of the fiscal year; April is the calendar-year date.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: The filing requirement under IRC § 6012 is measured against what?
options: Taxable income
Adjusted gross income
Gross income
Net income after credits
questions.explanation: A taxpayer whose deductions eliminate the liability may still be required to file.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: What does a timely filed Form 4868 obtain?
options: Six months more to file and to pay
An automatic six-month extension of time to file only
Four months to file, extendable by a further two
A waiver of interest on the unpaid balance
questions.explanation: Interest runs from the original due date and the failure-to-pay addition continues to accrue.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A United States citizen whose tax home and abode are outside the United States has what extension without applying?
options: None; an application is always required
To the fifteenth day of the sixth month following the close of the taxable year, for filing and
Six months, running after the ordinary extension expires
To 15 April of the second following year
questions.explanation: and the ordinary six-month extension runs concurrently with it, not after it.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A filing deadline falls on a day that is a legal holiday in the taxpayer's state but not in the District of Columbia. What is the effect?
options: The deadline moves to the next business day
The deadline is unchanged
The deadline moves only for taxpayers resident in that state
The taxpayer must file early
questions.explanation: IRC § 7503 defines "legal holiday" as a legal holiday in the District of Columbia.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A calendar-year individual taxpayer files Form 4868 by the original due date and it is accepted. What does this extension actually accomplish?
options: It extends both the time to file and the time to pay any tax owed
It extends the time to file the return but not the time to pay any tax owed
It extends the time to pay but requires the return to still be filed on the original due date
It waives any failure-to-pay penalty regardless of when the balance is paid
questions.explanation: Form 4868 grants an automatic extension of time to file (typically six months), but it does not extend the time to pay. Tax owed is still due by the original due date, and interest and the failure-to-pay penalty generally continue to accrue on any unpaid balance from that date.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer has $500 of net self-employment earnings for the year and no other income. Which statement is correct about the filing requirement?
options: No return is required because total income is below the standard filing-threshold amounts
A return is required because net self-employment earnings of $400 or more trigger a filing requirement regardless of the general gross-income thresholds
A return is required only if the taxpayer also owes income tax on the amount
A return is required only if the taxpayer received a Form 1099-NEC for the income
questions.explanation: Net self-employment earnings of $400 or more create a filing requirement on their own, to capture self-employment tax, independent of the general gross-income filing thresholds that apply to wage and other income.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A taxpayer is claimed as a dependent on someone else's return and has only unearned income (interest and dividends) for the year. Compared to a taxpayer who is not claimed as a dependent, how is this dependent's own filing requirement determined?
options: Using the same gross-income thresholds that apply to non-dependents
Using separate, generally lower thresholds specific to dependents, based on earned and unearned income
There is never a filing requirement for a dependent regardless of income
Only the person who claims the dependent has any filing obligation related to that income
questions.explanation: A dependent's filing requirement is measured against its own set of thresholds (which differ for earned income, unearned income, and combinations of the two), not the general thresholds that apply to a taxpayer who isn't claimed as a dependent.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which is not a requirement for head of household status?
options: The individual is unmarried or considered unmarried on the last day of the year
A qualifying dependent parent lives at the same residence as the taxpayer
The individual paid more than half the cost of keeping up the home
A qualifying person lived in the home for more than half the year
questions.explanation: For a parent, the test is whether the taxpayer maintains the household that is the parent's principal place of abode — the parent need not live with the taxpayer.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A taxpayer's spouse died in 2024. For which years may the taxpayer file as a qualifying surviving spouse, assuming a dependent child in the home and no remarriage?
options: 2024 only
2025 through 2027
questions.explanation: A joint return is available for the year of death itself; surviving spouse status covers the two taxable years after it.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: When is marital status determined?
options: On the first day of the taxable year
On the last day of the taxable year, or at the time of death if a spouse dies during the year
By the number of months married during the year
On the date the return is filed

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A married taxpayer files separately, has a child living with her all year, pays all household costs, and her husband moved out on 12 August. May she file as head of household?
options: Yes; she paid all the costs and the child lived with her
Yes, because they are separated in fact
No; the spouse must not have been a member of the household during the last six months of the year
No; head of household is never available to a married person
questions.explanation: The spouse's departure must precede the final six months, so a departure after 30 June fails the test for that year.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Neither spouse will sign a joint return and one spouse is a nonresident alien for part of the year. What follows?
options: A joint return may still be filed if the alien spouse consents
No joint return may be made, and the other spouse may be treated as not married for head of
Both spouses must file as single
The couple must file jointly by default
questions.explanation: Section 6013(a)(1) bars the joint return; § 2(b)(2)(B) treats the taxpayer as not married for head of household.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Dana's spouse died in 2024. Dana has not remarried and pays over half the cost of keeping up a home that is the principal residence of Dana's dependent child for all of 2026. Which filing status may Dana use for the 2026 tax return?
options: Single
Head of household
Qualifying surviving spouse
Married filing jointly
questions.explanation: Qualifying surviving spouse status is available for the two tax years following the year of a spouse's death (here, 2025 and 2026) if the taxpayer has not remarried, maintains a home that is the principal residence of a dependent child for the whole year, and paid over half the cost of keeping up that home. Head of household would apply once the two-year window has passed.
questions.pageTitle: Taxpayer filing status (e.g., single, head of household)

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A married couple lives together all year and wants to file separate returns. If one spouse itemizes deductions on Form 1040, what is required of the other spouse?
options: The other spouse may freely choose to itemize or claim the standard deduction
The other spouse must also itemize, even if it produces a $0 itemized total
The other spouse must claim the standard deduction
The couple must instead file a joint return
questions.explanation: Under MFS, if one spouse itemizes, the other spouse's standard deduction is treated as zero — the other spouse must also itemize (even if that means claiming little or nothing), rather than being free to claim the standard deduction.
questions.pageTitle: Taxpayer filing status (e.g., single, head of household)

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which of the following, by itself, disqualifies a taxpayer from claiming head of household status?
options: Being unmarried at the end of the year
Paying more than half the cost of keeping up the home
Living with a qualifying person for more than half the year
Filing a joint return with a spouse for the year
questions.explanation: Head of household requires the taxpayer to be unmarried (or considered unmarried) at year end and to file their own return; filing a joint return with a spouse is fundamentally incompatible with claiming head of household for that year. The other three items are requirements, not disqualifiers.
questions.pageTitle: Taxpayer filing status (e.g., single, head of household)

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which does not meet the age requirement to be a qualifying child?
options: A 17-year-old single mother
A 30-year-old with a permanent and total disability
A 28-year-old full-time student
A 9-year-old
questions.explanation: A student must be under 24; there is no age limit for an individual permanently and totally disabled at any time during the year.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A child resided with Parent A longer than with Parent B during the year, and Parent A also has the higher adjusted gross income. The parents do not file jointly and both claim the child. Who prevails?
options: Both may claim the child
Parent A
Parent B
Neither may claim the child
questions.explanation: decided by residence, not income. Income is reached only where residence is equal.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A dependent has $10,000 of taxable income and $4,000 of tax-exempt income, saves $1,000 and spends the rest on her own support. What is the minimum the taxpayer must provide?
questions.explanation: She applied $13,000 to her own support; the taxpayer must exceed half of total support, which means exceeding $13,000.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which individual may not be claimed as a dependent?
options: A foreign exchange student living in the taxpayer's home
A foreign-born adopted child living with the taxpayer as a member of the household
A resident of Canada
A United States resident alien
questions.explanation: The citizenship and residency gate admits residents of the United States, Canada and Mexico, with a narrow exception for an adopted child.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: An 18-year-old mother who can be claimed as a dependent by her parents lives with them and her own child. Who may claim the child?
options: Both the grandparents and the teenage parent
Neither
Only the grandparents
Only the teenage parent
questions.explanation: An individual who is a dependent of another taxpayer is treated as having no dependents — though the grandparents must also clear the tiebreaker rule that applies where no parent claims.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A taxpayer's 20-year-old child lived at home all year, is not a full-time student, and earned $9,000 in wages that the child spent on personal expenses. The taxpayer provided the rest of the child's support. Can the taxpayer claim the child as a dependent?
options: Yes, as a qualifying child, because the child lived at home all year
No, because a 20-year-old who is not a full-time student fails the qualifying child age test and is tested instead as a qualifying relative
Yes, automatically, because the taxpayer provided most of the child's support
No, because the child's own earnings disqualify the taxpayer regardless of the test used
questions.explanation: The qualifying child age test caps at under 19, or under 24 only if a full-time student (or any age if permanently and totally disabled). A 20-year-old non-student fails that test, so the child can only be a dependent as a qualifying relative — which requires the child's gross income to be under the exemption-amount threshold for the year. $9,000 of wages would need to be checked against that threshold before concluding either way; the point tested here is which test applies, not an assumed outcome.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Divorced parents Casey and Jordan do not file a joint return. Their child lived with Casey for 210 nights and with Jordan for 155 nights during the year, and both parents otherwise meet the requirements to claim the child. Absent a signed release (Form 8332) to the contrary, which parent may claim the child as a qualifying child?
options: Jordan, because Jordan has the lower adjusted gross income
Casey, because the child resided with Casey for the greater number of nights
Whichever parent claims the child first on a timely filed return
Neither parent, because the child must be claimed by mutual written agreement
questions.explanation: The tiebreaker rule for divorced or separated parents who don't file jointly awards the qualifying child to the parent with whom the child resided the greater number of nights during the year. Adjusted gross income only becomes the tiebreaker if the nights are exactly equal.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A taxpayer's elderly parent does not live with the taxpayer but the taxpayer pays for more than half of the parent's total support and the parent's gross income is under the qualifying-relative threshold. What test does the parent NOT need to satisfy that a non-relative living in the home would?
options: The gross income test
The support test
The member-of-household-or-relationship test, as it applies to a member of household requirement
The joint return test
questions.explanation: A qualifying relative must either be related to the taxpayer in one of the specified ways or live with the taxpayer all year as a member of the household. A parent satisfies this through the relationship prong and, unlike an unrelated person, does not also need to live in the taxpayer's home to qualify.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A nonresident alien individual has no wages subject to withholding. When is the return due for a calendar year?
options: 15 April
15 June
15 October
The 15th day of the fourth month
questions.explanation: A nonresident alien whose wages *are* subject to chapter 24 withholding files on the ordinary April date.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: What period does IRC § 7508 disregard for a member serving in a combat zone?
options: The period of service only
The period of service plus 90 days
The period of service, plus continuous qualified hospitalisation for an injury received there, plus
One year from the end of service
questions.explanation: and the disregard reaches interest, penalties, additional amounts and additions to tax as well as the filing date.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which extension covers the time to pay as well as the time to file?
options: The automatic six-month extension on Form 4868
The extension for a citizen or resident whose tax home and abode are outside the United States
Any extension requested before the due date
None; extensions never cover payment
questions.explanation: Regulation § 1.6081-5 extends both, and runs concurrently with the six-month extension.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A joint refund is reduced to satisfy one spouse's past-due child support. What is the other spouse's remedy?
options: Innocent spouse relief
An injured spouse claim allocating the joint refund
A collection due process hearing
Nothing; a joint refund is jointly owned
questions.explanation: Innocent spouse relief addresses liability for an understatement, which is a different question.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which statement about disaster relief under IRC § 7508A is correct?
options: Relief is available only where the Secretary issues a notice
There is both a discretionary period the Secretary may specify and a mandatory period
The liability is forgiven, not postponed
Relief applies only to the filing date, not to payment
questions.explanation: The mandatory period operates on the declaration's own dates whether or not a notice issues.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A United States person has signature authority over a foreign account belonging to their employer, with no financial interest in it. What must they file?
options: Neither the FBAR nor Form 8938
The FBAR only
Form 8938 only
Both
questions.explanation: The FBAR reaches signature or other authority over an account; § 6038D reaches an interest in an asset.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: When is the FBAR due?
options: 30 June, with no extension available
15 April, with an automatic extension to 15 October that need not be requested
With the income tax return, including any extension
31 December of the year reported
questions.explanation: The regulation at 31 C.F.R. § 1010.306(c) still states 30 June and is superseded.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: An unmarried taxpayer living in the United States held foreign assets worth $72,000 in July and $8,000 on 31 December. Is Form 8938 required?
options: No; the last-day value is below the threshold
Yes; the any-time value exceeds $75,000
No; the any-time value is below $75,000 and the last-day value is below $50,000
Yes; any foreign asset must be reported
questions.explanation: Both tests are below their thresholds — $72,000 does not exceed $75,000, and $8,000 does not exceed $50,000.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which is not reportable on an FBAR?
options: A foreign brokerage account producing no income
A foreign account emptied before year end
An account held in an IRA of which the taxpayer is the owner
A foreign account over which the taxpayer has only signature authority
questions.explanation: Accounts held in an IRA or a retirement plan of which the person is owner, beneficiary or participant are among the categories the IRS lists as not reportable.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Where is the FBAR filed?
options: Attached to the federal income tax return
With the IRS service centre for the taxpayer's district
Electronically with FinCEN through the BSA E-Filing System
With the Department of State
questions.explanation: It is not filed with the tax return.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which child is not subject to the kiddie tax?
options: A 16-year-old with substantial earned income and unearned income above the threshold
A 19-year-old full-time student whose earned income is one-third of their support
A 22-year-old full-time student whose earned income exceeds one-half of their support
A 12-year-old whose parents are both alive
questions.explanation: The earned income comparison applies to the over-18 limb, and exceeding half of support takes the child outside the rule; a child under 18 is within it regardless of earnings.
questions.pageTitle: Minor children's unearned income — the kiddie tax

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: How much unearned income may a child have in 2026 before any of it is taxed at the parent's rate?
questions.explanation: The definition of net unearned income subtracts the § 63(c)(5)(A) amount twice where the child does not itemise.
questions.pageTitle: Minor children's unearned income — the kiddie tax

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Income between the dependent standard deduction floor and the kiddie tax threshold is taxed at what rate?
options: Zero
The child's own rate
The parent's rate
The trust and estate rate
questions.explanation: Only net unearned income above the threshold reaches the parent's rate.
questions.pageTitle: Minor children's unearned income — the kiddie tax

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A child's only income is $6,000 of dividends, and backup withholding was applied to the account. May the parent elect to report the income on their own return?
options: Yes; the income is within the range and is only dividends
No; the election is unavailable where any amount has been withheld under the backup withholding
Yes, if the withholding is refunded first
Only if the child is under 18
questions.explanation: and the child should file anyway, because the withheld tax is recoverable only on the child's return.
questions.pageTitle: Minor children's unearned income — the kiddie tax

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Two children of the same parent each have net unearned income. How is the allocable parental tax computed?
options: Separately for each child
Once, on the parent's income including the net unearned income of all affected children, then
Only for the child with the larger amount
By adding the children's own tax liabilities
questions.pageTitle: Minor children's unearned income — the kiddie tax

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A 16-year-old dependent has $4,000 of interest income and no earned income for the year. Which statement about the kiddie tax rules is correct?
options: The kiddie tax cannot apply because the child is under 18
The kiddie tax can apply because the child is under 18 at year end, regardless of earned income
The kiddie tax only applies once the child turns 18
The kiddie tax applies only if the child files a joint return
questions.explanation: The kiddie tax age test is met for any child under age 18 at year end, without regard to how much earned income the child has. (The earned-income-versus-support comparison only comes into play for the 18, and 19–23 full-time student, age brackets.)

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A 19-year-old, full-time college student who is a dependent has $6,000 of earned income and $3,000 of unearned income, and the earned income is more than half of the student's own support for the year. Does the kiddie tax apply?
options: Yes, because the student is under 24
No, because a full-time student age 19–23 is only subject to the kiddie tax if earned income does NOT exceed half of the student's own support, and here it does
Yes, because the student has any unearned income at all
No, full-time students are always exempt from the kiddie tax
questions.explanation: For the 19–23 full-time-student bracket, the kiddie tax age test is met only when the student's earned income does NOT exceed half of their own support. Because this student's earned income does exceed half of their support, the age test for this bracket is not met, so the kiddie tax does not apply on that basis.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Parents want to report their young child's interest and dividend income directly on their own return instead of filing a separate return for the child. Which form supports that election, and which form is used if the parents do not make it?
options: Form 8814 to elect to include the child's income on the parents' return; Form 8615 on the child's own return if the election is not made
Form 8615 to elect to include the child's income on the parents' return; Form 8814 on the child's own return if the election is not made
Form 8332 for either option, depending on custodial status
Schedule 8812 for either option, depending on the amount of income
questions.explanation: Form 8814 (Parents' Election to Report Child's Interest and Dividends) lets qualifying parents include the child's investment income on their own return. If the parents don't make that election — or the child doesn't qualify for it — the child's own return computes the kiddie tax using Form 8615.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Which form reports health insurance obtained from a source other than the Marketplace?
options: Form 1095-A
Form 1095-B
Form 1095-C
All of these
questions.explanation: Form 1095-A comes from the Marketplace; Form 1095-C comes from an applicable large employer.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: What is the individual shared responsibility payment for 2026?
options: It is computed as a percentage of household income
It is the greater of a flat dollar amount or a percentage of income
Zero, because both limbs of the penalty computation now yield nothing
The requirement to maintain coverage was repealed, so there is none
questions.explanation: The requirement in § 5000A remains; only the penalty amounts were reduced to zero.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A taxpayer's household income is 415 percent of the poverty line for their family size in 2026, and they received advance premium tax credit payments. What follows?
options: A reduced credit computed on a percentage of income
No credit, and the advance payments are repayable
The credit is unaffected, because the ceiling was suspended
The credit is available but capped at the advance payments
questions.explanation: The suspension of the 400 percent ceiling applied only to taxable years beginning before 1 January 2026.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Excess advance premium tax credit payments in 2026 are repaid in what amount?
options: Limited by a cap that varies with household income
In full, regardless of household income
Only to the extent they exceed the credit by more than a stated amount
Not at all, if income was correctly projected at enrolment
questions.explanation: The limitation in § 36B(f)(2)(B) was removed for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: An employer averaged exactly 50 full-time employees during the preceding calendar year. Is it an applicable large employer?
options: No; the threshold is more than 50
Yes; the threshold is an average of at least 50
Only if it offers coverage
Only if the employees are in a single location

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: For purposes of computing the premium tax credit, whose income generally makes up 'household income' on Form 8962?
options: Only the taxpayer's own modified AGI
The modified AGI of the taxpayer, the taxpayer's spouse if filing jointly, and any dependents who are required to file a return
The modified AGI of every person listed on the Marketplace application, regardless of filing requirement
Gross income before any adjustments, for the taxpayer and spouse only
questions.explanation: Household income for the premium tax credit is the taxpayer's modified AGI plus the modified AGI of the spouse (if filing jointly) and of each dependent who is required to file a tax return for the year — not every dependent regardless of filing requirement.
questions.pageTitle: ACA requirements (e.g., health insurance coverage, total household income, advanced premium tax credit, household size)

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A taxpayer received advance premium tax credit payments during the year that turned out to exceed the premium tax credit actually allowed based on year-end income. What happens on the return?
options: The excess is always forgiven and requires no repayment
The excess advance payments are reconciled on Form 8962 and generally must be repaid, subject to any applicable repayment limitation based on income
The taxpayer must amend the Marketplace application instead of addressing it on the tax return
The excess is treated as an itemized deduction reduction with no other adjustment
questions.explanation: Form 8962 reconciles advance payments against the premium tax credit actually computed from year-end household income and family size. Excess advance payments generally must be repaid as additional tax, though the amount owed can be limited depending on income — the mechanics of that limitation are set by the current-year rules rather than fixed permanently in the statute.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Two separate tax families were both covered under a single Marketplace policy for part of the year (for example, divorced parents whose child is covered on one parent's policy while both parents are separate tax families). How is the premium tax credit computed for each family?
options: Only the policyholder may claim any premium tax credit for the policy
Each family computes its own credit independently with no allocation between them
The policy amounts (enrollment premium, applicable SLCSP premium, and advance payments) are allocated between the tax families, typically on Form 8962, Part IV
The premium tax credit is unavailable whenever more than one tax family is covered by the same policy
questions.explanation: When one Marketplace policy covers individuals from more than one tax family, the relevant policy amounts must be allocated between the families — commonly by an agreed percentage — using the shared policy allocation mechanics on Form 8962, rather than each family or only the policyholder claiming the credit unallocated.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A client receives $9,000 from a friend who describes it as a gift, and $400 of interest earned on the money after depositing it. What is includible?
drills.answer: the $400. The value of property acquired by gift is excluded from gross income (IRC § 102(a)), but IRC § 102(b)(1) provides that the exclusion does not extend to the income from that property. The interest is § 61(a)(4) income.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of all worldwide taxable and nontaxable income

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A United States citizen lived and worked in Portugal for the whole taxable year, was paid by a Portuguese employer, and received no United States information return. Is the salary reportable?
drills.answer: yes. All citizens of the United States, wherever resident, are liable to the income taxes imposed by the Code whether the income is received from sources within or without the United States (Reg. § 1.1-1(b)). Whether tax is ultimately due is a separate question — the § 911 exclusion and the foreign tax credit may reduce or eliminate it — but the salary is gross income and is reported.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of all worldwide taxable and nontaxable income

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A taxpayer receives $9,200 in cash tips during the year, all reported to the employer. Are the tips excluded from gross income?
drills.answer: no. Tips are compensation for services and so are gross income under IRC § 61(a)(1). What IRC § 224 provides is a deduction for qualified tips, subject to its own cap and income phase-out. Because the amount remains in gross income, it still enters adjusted gross income and still affects every threshold measured from it.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of all worldwide taxable and nontaxable income

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A lender forgives $40,000 of a taxpayer's home mortgage in 2026. The taxpayer is solvent and not in bankruptcy. Is the discharge includible?
drills.answer: yes. Discharge of indebtedness income is listed at IRC § 61(a)(11), and the qualified principal residence indebtedness exclusion in IRC § 108(a)(1)(E) reaches only discharges before 1 January 2026, or discharges under an arrangement entered into and evidenced in writing before that date. With neither the title 11 nor the insolvency exclusion available, the $40,000 is includible.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of all worldwide taxable and nontaxable income

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A sole proprietor pays health insurance premiums of $7,000 and has net earnings from the business of $4,200 after the deduction for half of self-employment tax. How much may she deduct under IRC § 162(l)?
drills.answer: $4,200. IRC § 162(l)(2)(A) caps the deduction at the taxpayer's earned income within § 401(c) derived from the trade or business with respect to which the plan is established. The remaining $2,800 is not deductible under § 162(l), though it may be a medical expense for itemized purposes.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of applicable exclusions and adjustments to gross income

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: Spouses file jointly. The husband is covered by a retirement plan at work; the wife is not. Are their two IRA deductions governed by the same phase-out range?
drills.answer: no. The husband, as an active participant, is governed by the IRC § 219(g)(3)(B)(i) joint range. The wife, who is not an active participant but is married to one, is governed by the separate and considerably higher range in IRC § 219(g)(7). The same joint income can therefore fully allow one spouse's deduction and eliminate the other's.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of applicable exclusions and adjustments to gross income

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A civilian employee moves across the country in 2026 for a new job and pays $6,500 in moving costs, unreimbursed. What is deductible?
drills.answer: nothing. IRC § 217(k)(1) provides that § 217 does not apply to any taxable year beginning after 31 December 2017 except for an individual to whom § 217(g) applies, and Pub. L. 119-21 § 70113(a) struck the 2026 end date, making the suspension permanent. Only a § 217(g) military move and, under new § 217(k)(2), a qualifying intelligence community relocation are excepted.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of applicable exclusions and adjustments to gross income

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: Why does it matter whether an amount is excluded from gross income rather than deducted in arriving at adjusted gross income, if both reduce tax by the same amount?
drills.answer: because only the exclusion keeps the amount out of gross income, and a great many provisions key off gross income or adjusted gross income rather than taxable income. An adjustment reduces adjusted gross income too, so on that axis the two behave alike — the sharper contrast is with a deduction taken after adjusted gross income, such as an itemized deduction or a § 63(b) deduction, which reduces taxable income while leaving every adjusted-gross-income threshold untouched.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of applicable exclusions and adjustments to gross income

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A single taxpayer, age 67 and not blind, is not a dependent of anyone. Which components make up her standard deduction, and what limits could reduce it?
drills.answer: the basic amount for an unmarried individual under IRC § 63(c)(2) as modified by § 63(c)(7), plus one aged increment under § 63(f)(1)(A) at the higher § 63(f)(3) rate for an unmarried individual who is not a surviving spouse. Nothing reduces it: § 63(c)(5) does not apply because no one claims her, and neither § 67 nor § 68 touches the standard deduction.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: Spouses file separately. One itemizes. The other has itemized deductions of $900 and would prefer the standard deduction. What is the second spouse's standard deduction?
drills.answer: zero. IRC § 63(c)(6)(A) sets the standard deduction at zero for a married individual filing a separate return where either spouse itemizes. The second spouse deducts the $900 of itemized deductions, and nothing else.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A taxpayer who does not elect to itemize gives $1,500 in cash to her parish and $400 to a donor advised fund. What, if anything, can she deduct?
drills.answer: up to the § 170(p) limit for her filing status, counting only the parish gift. IRC § 170(p) reaches cash contributions to a § 170(b)(1)(A) organization and expressly excludes gifts for the establishment or maintenance of a donor advised fund and gifts to a § 509(a)(3) supporting organization. The donor advised fund gift is deductible nowhere, since she has not elected to itemize.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A taxpayer's itemized deductions total $60,000 after each category limit. His taxable income, computed without § 68 and increased by that $60,000, exceeds the start of the top bracket by $40,000. What are his allowed itemized deductions?
drills.answer: $57,838. IRC § 68(a) reduces the total by 2/37 of the lesser of the itemized deductions ($60,000) or the taxable income above the top bracket threshold ($40,000) — so 2/37 of $40,000, or $2,162.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A high school swim coach spends her own money on team equipment, which before 2026 was a suspended miscellaneous itemized deduction. What changed?
drills.answer: IRC § 67(b)(13) now excludes educator expenses from miscellaneous itemized deductions, so the § 67(h) suspension does not reach them, and § 67(g) defines the term to include an interscholastic sports coach and to cover expenses incurred as part of instructional activity. She may claim them if she elects to itemize.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A taxpayer's qualifying child has an ITIN but no social security number. What credit, if any, is available for that child?
drills.answer: the credit for other dependents. IRC § 24(h)(7) denies the child tax credit without the child's social security number, but IRC § 24(h)(4)(C) treats a qualifying child denied the credit by reason of paragraph (7) as a dependent to whom the $500 credit for other dependents applies.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: Why can a nonrefundable credit be lost even though the taxpayer plainly qualifies for it?
drills.answer: because IRC § 26(a) caps the aggregate of the subpart A credits at regular tax liability reduced by the foreign tax credit allowable under § 27, plus the § 55(a) tax. Once other nonrefundable credits have absorbed that liability there is nothing left for the credit to offset, and subpart A credits do not produce a refund.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A married couple filing jointly paid $5,000 in tuition for one dependent undergraduate and $7,000 for another in a master's programme. Can they claim the American Opportunity credit for one and the Lifetime Learning credit for the other?
drills.answer: yes, but the two behave differently. The American Opportunity credit is computed per eligible student under IRC § 25A(b)(1), so it applies to the undergraduate on that student's own expenses. The Lifetime Learning credit under IRC § 25A(c)(1) is a percentage of expenses up to a single ceiling per return, not per student. IRC § 25A(c)(2)(A) prevents double-counting: expenses of a student for whom the American Opportunity credit is allowed are not taken into account under the Lifetime Learning subsection at all.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A client bought an electric vehicle in November 2025 and installed rooftop solar in February 2026. Which credits are available?
drills.answer: neither. IRC § 30D(h) denies the clean vehicle credit for any vehicle acquired after 30 September 2025, so the November purchase is outside it. IRC § 25D(h) provides that the residential clean energy credit does not apply to expenditures made after 31 December 2025, so the February installation is outside that. The two provisions use different dates and different tests, which is why each has to be checked on its own terms.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A taxpayer's prior-year tax was $18,000 on adjusted gross income of $210,000. This year's tax will be $30,000. What is the required annual payment?
drills.answer: $19,800. Under IRC § 6654(d)(1)(B) it is the lesser of 90 percent of this year's tax ($27,000) and 100 percent of last year's — but because prior-year adjusted gross income exceeded $150,000, IRC § 6654(d)(1)(C)(i) substitutes 110 percent, giving $19,800. That is the lesser figure and so the required annual payment.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of tax payments and refundable credits

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A taxpayer had no estimated payments and $12,000 withheld from a bonus paid in December. Is she treated as having paid nothing by the April installment date?
drills.answer: no. IRC § 6654(g)(1) deems the IRC § 31 credit to be a payment of estimated tax with an equal part paid on each due date, so a quarter of the $12,000 is treated as paid by the April date. She could displace that by establishing the actual withholding dates, but here the default is to her advantage and she would not want to.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of tax payments and refundable credits

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A single taxpayer aged 22 with no children has earned income well within the phase-out range. Does she qualify for the earned income credit?
drills.answer: no. IRC § 32(c)(1)(A)(ii)(II) requires an individual with no qualifying child to have attained age 25 but not 65 before the close of the taxable year. The temporary removal of the age floor in IRC § 32(n) applied only to taxable years beginning after 31 December 2020 and before 1 January 2022.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of tax payments and refundable credits

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A client claiming the earned income credit files electronically on 20 January and asks when the refund will arrive.
drills.answer: not before 15 February. IRC § 6402(m) bars any credit or refund of an overpayment before the 15th day of the second month following the close of the taxable year where a credit is allowed under § 32 or under § 24 by reason of subsection (d). The bar applies to the whole refund, not just the credit, so the rest of it is held too.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of tax payments and refundable credits

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A taxpayer receives a notice stating that additional tax is due because an entry on the return is inconsistent with another entry on the same return. May the taxpayer petition the Tax Court?
drills.answer: no. That is a mathematical or clerical error under IRC § 6213(g)(2)(C), so the notice is not a notice of deficiency and IRC § 6213(b)(1) expressly denies any right to petition the Tax Court on it. The taxpayer's route is a timely abatement request under IRC § 6213(b)(2)(A), after which any reassessment must follow the deficiency procedures and the Tax Court becomes available.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: During intake you learn from an account transcript that your new client omitted income from a return filed two years ago. What must you do?
drills.answer: advise the client promptly of the fact of the omission and of the consequences under the Code and regulations (Circular 230 § 10.21). The rule does not require you to correct the prior year or to withdraw; it requires the disclosure to the client, of both the fact and the consequences.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A client needs the return exactly as filed, including every attached schedule and statement. Which transcript should you order?
drills.answer: none of them. A transcript is not a photocopy of the return. A copy of the return as filed is requested on Form 4506 for a fee. The tax return transcript shows most line items from the original Form 1040-series return but does not reflect later changes, and the record of account combines the return and account transcripts rather than reproducing the filing.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: You hold a signed Form 8821 for a client's 2024 year. A different client asks you about a transaction with that first client, and the transcript would answer the question. May you use it?
drills.answer: no. IRC § 6103(c) permits disclosure to a designee but provides that the designee shall not use the information for any purpose other than the express purpose for which consent was granted, and shall not disclose it to another person without the taxpayer's express permission or request.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A client gives their daughter an interest in a family partnership that will not become possessory for ten years. The interest is worth $4,000. Is a gift tax return required?
drills.answer: yes. The IRC § 2503(b) annual exclusion applies only to gifts of present interests, so a gift of a future interest is not within the § 6019 exception however small it is. The return is required even though the value is well below the annual exclusion figure.
drills.pageTitle: Additional required returns filed and taxes paid

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A couple paid a housekeeper $2,600 in cash wages for the year, spread evenly across the four quarters. What employment filings arise?
drills.answer: none of the two main ones, but the tests must be run separately. The annual cash wage figure is below the social security and Medicare threshold, so no FICA applies. Quarterly wages of roughly $650 are below the unemployment tax threshold of more than $1,000 in any calendar quarter, so no FUTA applies either. Had the same total been paid in a single quarter, FUTA would have applied while FICA still would not.
drills.pageTitle: Additional required returns filed and taxes paid

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: Why can hiring a household employee produce a penalty on the individual income tax return?
drills.answer: because IRC § 3510(b)(1) provides that, solely for purposes of IRC § 6654, domestic service employment taxes are treated as a tax imposed by chapter 2 for the employer's taxable year. They therefore enter the required annual payment for estimated tax, and a taxpayer whose withholding was set for salary alone will be short. IRC § 3510(a)(3) removes any deposit obligation, so nothing during the year prompts payment.
drills.pageTitle: Additional required returns filed and taxes paid

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A client failed to file a required foreign trust information return. The trust's gross reportable amount is $900,000 and no additional tax is due. What is the exposure?
drills.answer: substantial, and unrelated to the tax. IRC § 6677(a) sets the penalty at the greater of a fixed amount or 35 percent of the gross reportable amount, so the percentage governs here. A further penalty applies if the failure continues more than 90 days after the Service mails notice. That the trust generated no additional tax is irrelevant to the computation.
drills.pageTitle: Additional required returns filed and taxes paid

drills.prompt: A restaurant adds an 18 percent charge to every bill for large parties and distributes it to servers. Is a server's share a qualified tip?
drills.answer: no. IRC § 224(d)(2)(A) requires the amount to be paid voluntarily without any consequence for non-payment, not to be the subject of negotiation, and to be determined by the payor. A compulsory charge set by the restaurant fails each limb. The share remains compensation for services under IRC § 61(a)(1) and is fully taxable; it simply cannot be deducted under § 224.
drills.pageTitle: Taxability of wages, salaries and other earnings

drills.prompt: An employee subject to the Fair Labor Standards Act works 50 hours in a week at a regular rate of $20, receiving $30 an hour for the ten extra hours. How much is qualified overtime compensation?
drills.answer: $100. IRC § 225(c)(1) reaches overtime required under section 7 of the Act only to the extent it is **in excess of the regular rate**. The premium is $10 an hour over the $20 regular rate, across ten hours. The other $200 is ordinary compensation.
drills.pageTitle: Taxability of wages, salaries and other earnings

drills.prompt: A married taxpayer with substantial qualified tips files separately because of a dispute with their spouse. What is the effect on the deduction?
drills.answer: it is lost entirely. IRC § 224(f) provides that where the taxpayer is a married individual within the meaning of § 7703, the section applies only if the taxpayer and spouse file a joint return. IRC § 225(e) does the same for overtime. This is a complete bar rather than a reduction, and it can outweigh whatever prompted the separate filing.
drills.pageTitle: Taxability of wages, salaries and other earnings

drills.prompt: A client's cash tips in March came to $14. Are they taxable, and must they be reported to the employer?
drills.answer: taxable yes, reported no. IRC § 3121(a)(12)(B) excludes cash tips of under $20 in a calendar month from wages, and IRC § 6053(a) requires reporting only of tips that are wages, so no statement is due for March. The tips remain compensation for services and so gross income under IRC § 61(a)(1), to be reported on the return.
drills.pageTitle: Taxability of wages, salaries and other earnings

drills.prompt: A client's municipal bond fund statement shows $8,000 of exempt-interest dividends, of which $1,200 is attributable to specified private activity bonds. What is reported?
drills.answer: the whole $8,000 as tax-exempt interest, none of it in gross income under IRC § 103(a), and $1,200 as an item of tax preference for alternative minimum tax purposes. IRC § 57(a)(5)(B) treats an exempt-interest dividend as interest on a specified private activity bond to the extent of its proportionate share of such interest received by the company paying it.

drills.prompt: Grandparents bought Series EE bonds in their granddaughter's name when she was born. She redeems them at 22 to pay tuition. Does IRC § 135 exclude the interest?
drills.answer: no. IRC § 135(c)(1)(B) requires the bond to have been issued to an individual who had attained age 24 **before the date of issuance**. A bond issued in a newborn's name can never satisfy that, whatever the proceeds are later spent on. Bonds registered to a parent aged over 24 at issue could have qualified.

drills.prompt: A cash-basis taxpayer holds a corporate bond with original issue discount and received no cash from it this year. Is anything includible?
drills.answer: yes. IRC § 1272(a)(1) includes in the holder's gross income the sum of the daily portions of the original issue discount for each day held during the taxable year, regardless of the method of accounting and regardless of whether anything was paid. The exceptions in § 1272(a)(2) — tax-exempt obligations among them — do not reach an ordinary corporate bond.

drills.prompt: A parent makes an $8,000 interest-free loan to a child, who uses it to buy a car. Does IRC § 7872 apply?
drills.answer: no. IRC § 7872(c)(2)(A) provides that the section does not apply to any day on which the aggregate outstanding amount of gift loans directly between the individuals does not exceed the de minimis figure, and $8,000 is below it. Had the child used the loan to buy income-producing assets, IRC § 7872(c)(2)(B) would disapply the exception and the section would operate.

drills.prompt: A corporation with $20,000 of accumulated earnings and profits and no current earnings and profits distributes $50,000 to a sole shareholder whose basis is $18,000. How is it characterised?
drills.answer: $20,000 is a dividend included in gross income (IRC § 316(a)(1), § 301(c)(1)); $18,000 is applied against and reduces basis to zero (IRC § 301(c)(2)); and the remaining $12,000 is treated as gain from the sale or exchange of property (IRC § 301(c)(3)(A)).
drills.pageTitle: Dividends and other distributions from mutual funds, corporations, and other entities

drills.prompt: A shareholder buys stock on 1 March, the ex-dividend date is 20 March, and she sells on 10 May. Are the dividends qualified?
drills.answer: yes. The 121-day period begins 60 days before 20 March, so on 19 January. Counting from 2 March — the day of acquisition is excluded under IRC § 246(c)(3)(A) — to the 10 May disposition is 70 days, which is more than the 60 days required by IRC § 1(h)(11)(B)(iii)(I) as it applies § 246(c).
drills.pageTitle: Dividends and other distributions from mutual funds, corporations, and other entities

drills.prompt: A client bought fund shares in November and received a capital gain dividend in December. Is the gain short-term?
drills.answer: no. IRC § 852(b)(3)(B) provides that a capital gain dividend is treated by shareholders as gain from the sale or exchange of a capital asset **held for more than one year**, whatever the shareholder's actual holding period in the fund shares. IRC § 854(a) separately keeps it out of qualified dividend income.
drills.pageTitle: Dividends and other distributions from mutual funds, corporations, and other entities

drills.prompt: Why can a taxpayer's own qualified dividend figure differ from the one the broker reports?
drills.answer: because the test in IRC § 1(h)(11)(B)(iii) is applied to the shareholder's holding period against each ex-dividend date, and the broker cannot always see whether a disposition broke it. The reported figure is a starting point; where the client sold within the window the qualified amount must be reduced on the return.
drills.pageTitle: Dividends and other distributions from mutual funds, corporations, and other entities

drills.prompt: A taxpayer in the business of renting construction equipment nets $40,000. Is the profit subject to self-employment tax?
drills.answer: yes. IRC § 1402(a)(1) excludes from net earnings from self-employment only rentals from real estate and from personal property **leased with the real estate**. Construction equipment let on its own is outside the exclusion, so a rental business in personal property produces net earnings from self-employment in the ordinary way.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer lets a boat occasionally, without profit motive, receiving $2,000 and spending $3,500. What is deductible?
drills.answer: nothing beyond deductions allowable regardless of profit motive. IRC § 183(b)(1) preserves those; the rest fall under § 183(b)(2), which would allow them only to the extent income exceeds the first tier — and they are miscellaneous itemized deductions, which IRC § 67(h) disallows for any taxable year beginning after 31 December 2017. The $2,000 is taxed with effectively nothing against it.

drills.prompt: Why is it wrong to report a for-profit but non-business equipment rental on a business schedule?
drills.answer: because it mischaracterises the activity in a way that costs money. A trade or business produces net earnings from self-employment; a non-business activity held for the production of income does not. The expenses are not lost by reporting correctly — IRC § 212 allows them and IRC § 62(a)(4) places deductions attributable to property held for the production of rents above the line — so the correct route gives the same deduction without the employment tax.

drills.prompt: A source states that hobby expenses become deductible again from 2026 under IRC § 67(g). What is wrong with it?
drills.answer: both halves. Pub. L. 119-21 § 70110(a) struck the 2026 end date, so the suspension of miscellaneous itemized deductions is permanent rather than expiring. And § 70110(b)(2) redesignated the suspension as IRC § 67(h), while a new § 67(g) now defines educator expenses for the purposes of § 67(b)(13). The citation and the conclusion are each out of date.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer who itemizes has $40,000 of gambling winnings and $50,000 of gambling losses in 2026. What is the deduction?
drills.answer: $40,000. IRC § 165(d)(1)(A) limits the deduction to 90 percent of losses, which is $45,000, and § 165(d)(1)(B) limits it to gains, which is $40,000. The deduction is the lesser of the two, so the gains limit governs here and the percentage cap does not bite. Net taxable gambling income is nil.

drills.prompt: Same taxpayer, but winnings and losses are each $50,000. What is the deduction, and why does the answer differ?
drills.answer: $45,000, leaving $5,000 of taxable income. Ninety percent of $50,000 is $45,000, which is below the $50,000 gains limit, so the percentage cap governs. The difference from the first question is that the percentage attaches to losses — once losses no longer exceed gains by more than a ninth, the percentage cap becomes the binding one.

drills.prompt: A recreational gambler wins $1,600 on a slot machine in 2026 and receives no Form W-2G. Is the amount taxable?
drills.answer: yes, in full. The IRC § 6041(a) reporting threshold for the calendar year is above that amount, so the payer had no filing obligation, and the Form W-2G instructions confirm the former separate figure for slot machines no longer applies. The threshold governs the payer's duty, not the character of the receipt, and the winnings are gross income under IRC § 61(a).

drills.prompt: A professional gambler argues that entry fees are business expenses under IRC § 162 and so fall outside the wagering limitation. Is that right?
drills.answer: no. IRC § 165(d)(2) provides that "losses from wagering transactions" includes any deduction otherwise allowable under this chapter incurred in carrying on any wagering transaction. Entry fees incurred in carrying on the activity are therefore inside the limitation and are subject to both ceilings. The rule applied only from 2018 to 2025 as originally enacted; Pub. L. 119-21 § 70114(a) removed the expiry.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer's property secures a nonrecourse debt of $180,000 and has an adjusted basis of $120,000. The lender forecloses when the property is worth $150,000. What are the consequences?
drills.answer: $60,000 of gain and no discharge of indebtedness income. Reg. § 1.1001-2(a)(4)(i) treats the disposition of property securing a nonrecourse liability as discharging the transferor from it, and Reg. § 1.1001-2(a)(1) includes the full liability in the amount realized — so $180,000 less the $120,000 basis. The property's $150,000 value is irrelevant to the computation.
drills.pageTitle: Tax treatment of forgiveness of debt

drills.prompt: A taxpayer with liabilities of $400,000 and assets worth $370,000 immediately before a discharge has $50,000 of debt forgiven outside bankruptcy. How much is excluded?
drills.answer: $30,000. IRC § 108(d)(3) measures insolvency as the excess of liabilities over the fair market value of assets immediately before the discharge, which is $30,000, and IRC § 108(a)(3) caps the exclusion at that amount. The remaining $20,000 is includible, and the excluded $30,000 reduces tax attributes under IRC § 108(b)(2).
drills.pageTitle: Tax treatment of forgiveness of debt

drills.prompt: A federal student loan balance is forgiven in February 2026 at the end of an income-driven repayment plan. Is it excluded?
drills.answer: no. The broad exclusion for any student loan discharge applied to discharges in 2021 through 2025; Pub. L. 119-21 § 70119 amended IRC § 108(f)(5) generally, and § 70119(c) applies the amendment to discharges after 31 December 2025. What remains is death or total and permanent disability under § 108(f)(5), and work-in-profession forgiveness under § 108(f)(1). Neither reaches an income-driven repayment discharge, so the general § 108(a) exclusions are the only route.
drills.pageTitle: Tax treatment of forgiveness of debt

drills.prompt: A taxpayer excludes $90,000 under the insolvency exclusion and holds a general business credit carryover. By how much is that carryover reduced?
drills.answer: by 33⅓ cents for each dollar excluded that reaches it. IRC § 108(b)(3)(A) sets the general rate at a dollar per dollar, but § 108(b)(3)(B) applies 33⅓ cents per dollar to the reductions in subparagraphs (B), (C) and (G) of § 108(b)(2) — the general business credit, minimum tax credit and foreign tax credit carryovers. The order in § 108(b)(2) still governs which attributes are reached first, net operating losses coming before the credit.
drills.pageTitle: Tax treatment of forgiveness of debt

drills.prompt: A citizen abroad excludes the maximum foreign earned income and also claims a credit for all the foreign tax paid on her salary. What is wrong?
drills.answer: the credit. IRC § 911(d)(6) denies any deduction, exclusion or credit — expressly including a credit for foreign taxes — to the extent it is properly allocable to or chargeable against amounts excluded under § 911(a). The foreign tax attributable to the excluded salary is therefore not creditable. Only tax on income actually included may be credited.
drills.pageTitle: Tax treatment of a U.S. citizen or resident with foreign income

drills.prompt: A resident alien is present in foreign countries for 340 full days across a 12-month period straddling two tax years. Can she use the foreign earned income exclusion?
drills.answer: yes, by the physical presence route. IRC § 911(d)(1)(B) applies to a citizen **or resident** of the United States present in a foreign country or countries for at least 330 full days in any period of 12 consecutive months, and the period need not align with a taxable year. She could not use the bona fide residence route in § 911(d)(1)(A), which is open to citizens only.
drills.pageTitle: Tax treatment of a U.S. citizen or resident with foreign income

drills.prompt: A taxpayer pays $9,000 of foreign tax but the IRC § 904(a) limitation allows a credit of only $5,500. What happens to the balance?
drills.answer: it carries. IRC § 904(c) deems the excess paid in the first preceding taxable year and then in any of the first ten succeeding taxable years, in that order, to the extent the limitation in that year exceeds the foreign taxes for it. The $3,500 is not lost, though it is only usable to the extent a carryback or carryover year has spare limitation.
drills.pageTitle: Tax treatment of a U.S. citizen or resident with foreign income

drills.prompt: A client wants to take a treaty position reducing United States tax on a foreign pension, and asks whether disclosure is necessary given that no tax will be due.
drills.answer: yes. IRC § 6114(a) requires disclosure by each taxpayer who takes the position that a treaty overrules or otherwise modifies an internal revenue law, on the return or, if none is required, in the form prescribed. The absence of tax is not an exception. IRC § 6712(a) imposes a penalty for each failure, which the Secretary may waive for reasonable cause under § 6712(b).
drills.pageTitle: Tax treatment of a U.S. citizen or resident with foreign income

drills.prompt: A degree candidate receives a $20,000 scholarship, spending $14,000 on tuition, $1,200 on books required for her courses, and $4,800 on rent. How much is includible?
drills.answer: $4,800. IRC § 117(b)(2) limits qualified tuition and related expenses to tuition and fees required for enrolment and to fees, books, supplies and equipment required for courses of instruction. The tuition and the required books qualify; rent is not a qualified expense however necessary it is to attending.

drills.prompt: A graduate student receives $12,000 conditioned on serving as a research assistant, and spends all of it on tuition. Is it excluded?
drills.answer: no. IRC § 117(c)(1) provides that the exclusion does not apply to that portion of any amount received which represents payment for teaching, research or other services by the student. Spending it on tuition is irrelevant — the service condition removes it from the exclusion before the qualified-expense test is reached, and none of the three § 117(c)(2) exceptions covers a university assistantship.

drills.prompt: A photographer and a caterer swap services, each valuing their own work at $1,500. What is reportable?
drills.answer: each includes $1,500 as compensation. Reg. § 1.61-2(d)(1) provides that where services are paid for in exchange for other services, the fair market value of the services taken in payment must be included in income, and a stipulated price is presumed to be fair market value absent evidence to the contrary. Each may also have a business deduction for the services received, but the income arises on both sides and no information return will report it.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer wins a $25,000 award for civic achievement, having been nominated by others, and donates it to a qualifying charity a week after receiving it. Is it excluded under IRC § 74(b)?
drills.answer: no. IRC § 74(b)(3) requires the prize to be **transferred by the payor** to a governmental unit or a § 170(c)(1) or (2) organisation pursuant to a designation made by the recipient. Receiving the money and then donating it fails that condition, however quickly it is done. The award is included in gross income under § 74(a), and the donation is a charitable contribution deduction subject to its own limits.

drills.prompt: A cash-basis consultant receives a cheque on 30 December and deposits it on 6 January. In which year is the income reported?
drills.answer: the earlier year. Under Reg. § 1.451-2(a) income is constructively received when made available so that the taxpayer may draw upon it at any time. The cheque was in hand and nothing restricted her control of it — choosing when to deposit is not a substantial limitation or restriction.

drills.prompt: A savings account credits interest on 31 December, but the bank requires 30 days' notice before any withdrawal. Is the interest constructively received?
drills.answer: yes. Reg. § 1.451-2(a)(4) provides that a requirement to give notice of intention to withdraw in advance is not a substantial limitation or restriction. The same paragraph adds that where the rate payable depends on the amount of notice given, earnings at the maximum rate are constructively received.

drills.prompt: A corporation declares a dividend payable on 31 December and, following its usual practice, mails cheques that shareholders receive in January. When is it income?
drills.answer: in January. Reg. § 1.451-2(b) states this case expressly — although dividends are constructively received when unqualifiedly made subject to the shareholder's demand, a dividend declared payable on 31 December and paid by the corporation's usual practice of mailing cheques that arrive the following January is not considered constructively received in December.
