drills.pageTitle: Nonbusiness casualty and theft losses in declared disaster areas

drills.prompt: What is required for a State declared disaster?
drills.answer: A determination by the Governor of the State, or the Mayor for the District of Columbia, **and by the Secretary**, that the event causes damage of sufficient severity and magnitude to warrant applying the section (IRC § 165(h)(5)(C)(i)).
drills.pageTitle: Nonbusiness casualty and theft losses in declared disaster areas

drills.prompt: A taxpayer pays 5,000 dollars in investment management fees in 2026. How much is deductible?
drills.answer: None. The fees are not within the IRC § 67(b) list, so they are miscellaneous itemized deductions, and § 67(h) allows no miscellaneous itemized deduction for any taxable year beginning after 2017 — permanently, since Pub. L. 119-21 § 70110 struck the end date.

drills.prompt: Are gambling losses miscellaneous itemized deductions?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 67(b)(3) excludes losses described in § 165(d) from the definition, so they survive the disallowance — though they remain subject to the § 165(d) ceiling.

drills.prompt: A beneficiary includes 120,000 dollars of income in respect of a decedent in 2026. What deduction may be available?
drills.answer: The IRC § 691(c)(1)(A) deduction for the federal estate tax attributable to that item, claimed in the year of inclusion and preserved from the disallowance by § 67(b)(7).

drills.prompt: A taxpayer repays 50,000 dollars in 2026 that was taxed in 2022. What does IRC § 1341 provide?
drills.answer: The tax for 2026 is the lesser of the tax computed with the deduction, or the tax computed without it reduced by the decrease in the 2022 tax that excluding the item would have produced (§ 1341(a)(4), (5)) — a computation, not an election.

drills.prompt: Why does the § 67(b) list matter more now than when it was written?
drills.answer: Because § 67(h) disallows every itemized deduction that is not on it. The list was drafted in 1986 to identify deductions escaping a 2 percent floor; since 2018 it has defined which itemized deductions exist at all.

drills.prompt: What is a nonresident alien individual's standard deduction?
drills.answer: Zero. IRC § 63(c)(6)(B) lists a nonresident alien individual among the classes for which the standard deduction is zero.

drills.prompt: May a nonresident alien deduct expenses against United States dividend income taxed at the flat rate?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 873(a) allows deductions only for purposes of § 871(b), which taxes effectively connected income; § 871(a) taxes fixed or determinable income on the gross amount.

drills.prompt: Which deductions are allowed without any connection to effectively connected income?
drills.answer: Three, under IRC § 873(b) — casualty and theft losses within § 165(c)(2) or (3) for property located in the United States, charitable contributions under § 170, and one personal exemption under § 151 unless the taxpayer is a resident of a contiguous country or a United States national.

drills.prompt: A nonresident alien donates to a charity organised in their home country. Is it deductible?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 170(c)(2)(A) requires the donee to be created or organised in the United States or a possession, or under United States, State, District of Columbia or possession law.

drills.prompt: How is a student on an F-1 visa with no United States business treated?
drills.answer: As engaged in a United States trade or business, by IRC § 871(c), with the income described in the second sentence of § 1441(b) treated as effectively connected to the extent derived from United States sources — which brings § 871(b) rates and § 873(a) deductions into play.

drills.prompt: A single taxpayer with taxable income of $140,000 runs a law practice with $110,000 of qualified business income and pays no wages. What is the § 199A deduction, and does the practice being a specified service trade or business matter?
drills.answer: $22,000, and no. Taxable income is below the threshold, so IRC § 199A(b)(3)(A) applies the per-business rule without the wage and property limitation and § 199A(d)(3)(A) treats the specified service business as qualified in full — subject only to the § 199A(a)(2) ceiling.

drills.prompt: A partnership pays a partner a $90,000 guaranteed payment for services and pays $200,000 of W-2 wages to its employees. How does the guaranteed payment affect that partner's qualified business income and the partnership's W-2 wages for the limitation?
drills.answer: It reduces the partner's qualified business income — IRC § 199A(c)(4)(B) excludes a § 707(c) guaranteed payment — and does nothing for the wage limitation, because a guaranteed payment is not a W-2 wage under § 6051(a) and is not in the $200,000. The partner loses on both sides.

drills.prompt: Why can a rental real estate business with a single part-time employee still claim a substantial deduction above the threshold?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 199A(b)(2)(B)(ii) offers the alternative of 25 percent of W-2 wages plus 2.5 percent of the unadjusted basis of all qualified property, and the taxpayer takes the greater of that and 50 percent of wages. A capital-intensive business with little payroll is carried by the basis component, which depreciation does not reduce.

drills.prompt: A married couple filing jointly have $3,000 of qualified business income from a craft business in which they both materially participate, and taxable income well below the threshold. What is their deduction?
drills.answer: $600 by the ordinary computation, but IRC § 199A(i) makes it $400 or the computed amount, whichever is greater — so $600 stands. The floor would apply only if 20 percent of QBI came to less than $400, which needs QBI below $2,000; they clear the $1,000 applicable-taxpayer test either way.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer's only business income is $40,000 of qualified publicly traded partnership income. The partnership reports no allocable W-2 wages. Does the wage limitation reduce the deduction?
drills.answer: No. Qualified publicly traded partnership income enters the combined qualified business income amount through IRC § 199A(b)(1)(B) at a flat 20 percent, outside the § 199A(b)(2) per-business computation where the wage and property limitation lives. Qualified REIT dividends are treated the same way.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer pays a neighbour to watch her 6-year-old while she does unpaid volunteer work at a food bank two days a week and works at a paid job three days a week. Which expenses are employment-related?
drills.answer: Only those for the three paid days. Reg. § 1.21-1(c)(1) states that work as a volunteer or for nominal consideration is not gainful employment, and § 1.21-1(c)(2)(i) requires expenses covering a period only partly employed to be allocated on a daily basis.

drills.prompt: A married couple file separately. One spouse maintained a home that was the principal place of abode of their 5-year-old for the whole year, paid over half the cost of it, and the other spouse moved out in March. May that spouse claim the credit?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 21(e)(2) requires a joint return, but § 21(e)(4) treats a married individual as not married where all three of its conditions are met — the home test, the over-half-the-cost test, and the absence of the other spouse for the last six months of the year. A March departure satisfies the third.

drills.prompt: Why can a taxpayer who pays $10,000 for the care of three children never take a credit on more than a fraction of it?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 21(c) caps creditable employment-related expenses at $6,000 where there are two or more qualifying individuals. The cap is pooled rather than per child, so a third child adds nothing, and the cap is further reduced by any amount excluded under § 129.

drills.prompt: A grandmother is paid $4,000 to care for her daughter's child. The grandmother is her daughter's dependent. May the daughter claim the credit?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 21(e)(6)(A) denies the credit for any amount paid to an individual with respect to whom a dependency deduction is allowable to the taxpayer or the taxpayer's spouse. Paying a dependent — or the taxpayer's own child under 19 — never produces a credit, whatever the amount or the market rate.

drills.prompt: What is the maximum credit for a single taxpayer with one qualifying individual, adjusted gross income of $300,000, and $5,000 of qualifying expenses?
drills.answer: $600. Expenses are capped at $3,000 for one qualifying individual under IRC § 21(c), and the applicable percentage cannot fall below 20 percent under § 21(a)(2)(B) however high adjusted gross income rises. There is no complete phase-out of this credit.

drills.prompt: A single taxpayer with modified adjusted gross income of $214,300 has two qualifying children. What is the credit before any refundability analysis?
drills.answer: $3,700. The credit starts at $4,400. Modified adjusted gross income exceeds the § 24(h)(3) threshold of $200,000 by $14,300, which is fourteen full thousands and a fraction, so fifteen steps of $50 apply — a reduction of $750. Note that the fraction counts as a whole step under § 24(b)(1).
drills.pageTitle: Child tax credit and credit for other dependents

drills.prompt: A married couple have earned income of $6,000, no tax liability, and three qualifying children. How much of the credit is refundable?
drills.answer: $525. Fifteen percent of earned income above $2,500 — 15 percent of $3,500 — is $525, and that is far below both the unused credit and the per-child cap, so it controls. The alternative in § 24(d)(1)(B)(ii) for three or more children uses social security taxes less the § 32 credit, which on these facts is unlikely to be larger.
drills.pageTitle: Child tax credit and credit for other dependents

drills.prompt: Why does a taxpayer's 19-year-old dependent son, a full-time student living at home, produce only a small credit?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 24(c)(1) requires a qualifying child to be under 17 at the close of the calendar year. He is a qualifying child under § 152(c)(3)(A)(ii) as a student under 24, but not one described in § 24(c), so § 24(h)(4)(A) treats him as an other dependent worth $500, nonrefundable.
drills.pageTitle: Child tax credit and credit for other dependents

drills.prompt: A return claims two children. One has a social security number issued in March, after the April due date passed unextended. What is the consequence?
drills.answer: No child tax credit for that child, because § 24(h)(7)(B)(ii) requires the number to be issued before the return's due date. Section 24(h)(4)(C) then treats that child as a dependent eligible for the $500 other-dependent amount. The other child's credit is unaffected.
drills.pageTitle: Child tax credit and credit for other dependents

drills.prompt: A taxpayer's child tax credit was disallowed three years ago on a final determination that the claim was due to reckless disregard of the rules. May the taxpayer claim it this year?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 24(g)(1)(B)(ii) sets the disallowance period at two taxable years after the most recent year for which there was such a determination, and three years have passed. Ten years would apply had the determination been one of fraud.
drills.pageTitle: Child tax credit and credit for other dependents

drills.prompt: A taxpayer with a gross tax liability of $400 is entitled to the full American Opportunity credit for one student. What refund does the credit produce?
drills.answer: $840. IRC § 25A(i) makes 40 percent of the credit refundable, and the nonrefundable part first reduces the liability. The credit is $2,500; $400 offsets the tax; 40 percent of the remaining $2,100 is $840, which is under the $1,000 per-student ceiling.

drills.prompt: A student is in their fifth year of an undergraduate degree. Their parents claimed the American Opportunity credit for each of the first four years. What is available in year five?
drills.answer: The Lifetime Learning credit only. IRC § 25A(b)(2)(A) bars the election where such an election was in effect for the student — by the taxpayer or any other individual — for any four prior taxable years. The Lifetime Learning credit has no year limit.

drills.prompt: Why does a $6,000 scholarship reduce a $7,600 tuition bill to $1,600 of qualified expenses rather than reducing the credit by $6,000?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 25A(g)(2) operates on the expenses "before the application of subsections (b), (c), and (d)". The scholarship shrinks the base to which the credit formulas apply, and it does so before the income phase-out as well.

drills.prompt: A married couple file separately. One spouse paid $9,000 of tuition for a job-skills course. What credit is available?
drills.answer: None. IRC § 25A(g)(6) provides that where the taxpayer is a married individual within § 7703, the section applies only if the taxpayer and spouse file a joint return. There is no living-apart exception here.

drills.prompt: Three children of one household are each full-time first-year degree students with $4,000 of tuition. The parents' income is below the phase-out. How much larger is the American Opportunity credit than the Lifetime Learning credit would be?
drills.answer: $5,500 larger. The American Opportunity credit is per student — $2,500 each, or $7,500 — while the Lifetime Learning credit is 20 percent of a maximum of $10,000 per return, or $2,000, however many students there are.

drills.prompt: A single taxpayer's only foreign income is $2,900 of dividends from a foreign mutual fund reported on Form 1099-DIV, with $265 of foreign tax withheld. What is the simplest correct treatment?
drills.answer: Elect under IRC § 904(j). All foreign source gross income is qualified passive income shown on a payee statement and the tax is under the $300 single-filer ceiling, so the § 904(a) limitation does not apply and the full $265 is credited without a Form 1116. The cost is that no carryback or carryforward is available for that year.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer with US tax of $40,000, entire taxable income of $200,000 and foreign source taxable income of $25,000 paid $8,000 of foreign tax. What is credited this year?
drills.answer: $5,000. The IRC § 904(a) limitation is $40,000 multiplied by the ratio of $25,000 to $200,000. The remaining $3,000 carries back one taxable year and then forward up to ten under § 904(c), within the same basket.

drills.prompt: Why can a taxpayer with unused credits in the passive basket not apply them against US tax on general category income?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 904(d)(1) applies subsections (a), (b) and (c) separately to each category. The separate application governs the carryback and carryforward as well, so the excess stays in the passive basket for its whole life.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer paid $4,000 of foreign income tax and also paid a foreign value added tax of $900 on purchases. What is creditable?
drills.answer: The $4,000 only. IRC § 901(b) allows a credit for income, war profits and excess profits taxes, and § 903 extends that only to a tax paid in lieu of an income tax otherwise generally imposed. A value added tax is neither, so it is not creditable — though it may be deductible if it is a business expense.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer deducted foreign income taxes on an original return and now wants the credit instead, four years later. Is it too late?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 901(a) allows the choice to be made or changed at any time before the refund claim period expires, and § 6511(d)(3)(A) gives ten years from the due date of the return for the year the taxes were paid or accrued. Switching also triggers § 275(a)(4), so the deduction must be given up entirely for that year.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer with two qualifying children has earned income of $24,000, adjusted gross income of $29,500 including unemployment compensation, and $600 of tax-exempt interest. Which figure drives the phase-out, and does the interest matter?
drills.answer: Adjusted gross income of $29,500, because IRC § 32(a)(2)(B) uses the greater of adjusted gross income and earned income. The tax-exempt interest is disqualified income under § 32(i)(2)(B), but $600 is far below the ceiling, so it does not deny the credit.

drills.prompt: A married taxpayer lived apart from their spouse from March onwards, has a qualifying child who lived with them for the whole year, and files separately. Is the credit available?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 32(d)(2)(B) treats the individual as not married where they do not file jointly, reside with a qualifying child for more than half the year, and do not share a principal place of abode with the spouse during the last six months of the year. A March separation satisfies the third element.

drills.prompt: Why does releasing a dependency exemption to a noncustodial parent not move the earned income credit?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 32(c)(3)(A) applies § 152(c) determined without regard to § 152(e), the special rule for divorced parents. The child remains a qualifying child of the parent with whom they reside, so the earned income credit stays with the custodial parent even though the child tax credit moves.

drills.prompt: A preparer computes an earned income credit and a child tax credit on the same return and fails to file Form 8867. How many penalties?
drills.answer: Two. Section 6695(g) imposes the penalty for each failure to meet the due diligence requirements with respect to each benefit listed in it, and both credits are listed. There is no maximum on the aggregate.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer's earned income credit was disallowed two years ago in a deficiency proceeding, with no finding of fraud or recklessness. What must they do to claim it now?
drills.answer: Provide the information the Secretary requires to demonstrate eligibility — Form 8862 — under IRC § 32(k)(2). No disallowance period applies, because § 32(k)(1) bars the credit only after a final determination of fraud or of reckless or intentional disregard of the rules.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer paid $9,000 of qualified adoption expenses in 2025 for a domestic adoption that became final in 2027. On which return is the credit claimed?
drills.answer: The 2026 return. IRC § 23(a)(2)(A) allows a credit for an expense paid before the year the adoption becomes final in the taxable year *following* the year of payment. Finalisation in 2027 does not delay it, and no finalisation at all would not undo it.

drills.prompt: The same facts, but the child is not a citizen or resident of the United States. When is the credit claimed?
drills.answer: On the 2027 return. IRC § 23(e)(1) allows nothing for a foreign adoption unless it becomes final, and § 23(e)(2) then treats every expense paid earlier as paid in the year of finalisation.

drills.prompt: A couple adopt a child with special needs and pay $1,900 of qualified adoption expenses. Their income is well below the phase-out. Is the credit $1,900?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 23(a)(3) treats them as having paid the excess of the statutory special needs amount over the expenses actually paid in that year and all prior years, so the credit reaches the full statutory figure for 2026 regardless of the $1,900.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer's nonrefundable adoption credit exceeds their tax liability by $3,000. What happens to the excess?
drills.answer: It carries forward under IRC § 23(c)(1) and is added to the credit for the succeeding year, for up to five taxable years after the year the credit arose, used first in first out under § 23(c)(2). The refundable portion under § 23(a)(4) is not part of this and is paid out directly.

drills.prompt: An employer reimburses $4,000 of an employee's adoption expenses under a qualifying programme, and the employee paid $9,000 in total. What are the qualified adoption expenses for the credit?
drills.answer: $5,000. IRC § 23(d)(1)(D) excludes expenses reimbursed under an employer programme or otherwise. The reimbursed $4,000 may instead be excluded from gross income under § 137, subject to that section's own limit and phase-out, so the taxpayer gets both benefits but not on the same dollars.

drills.prompt: A married couple with two children have household income of 410 percent of the federal poverty line and received $9,000 of advance payments. What is the consequence at reconciliation for 2026?
drills.answer: The entire $9,000 is added to tax. They are not applicable taxpayers under IRC § 36B(c)(1)(A) because household income exceeds 400 percent of the poverty line, the temporary rule in § 36B(c)(1)(E) expired with taxable year 2025, and the repayment limitation in § 36B(f)(2)(B) was struck by Pub. L. 119-21 § 71305 for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025.

drills.prompt: An employee is offered an employer plan costing 6 percent of household income for self-only coverage, which pays 55 percent of allowed benefit costs. Can the employee claim the credit for Exchange coverage?
drills.answer: Yes, assuming the other conditions are met. The plan is affordable, but IRC § 36B(c)(2)(C)(ii) provides that an employee is not treated as eligible for minimum essential coverage where the plan's share of total allowed costs is less than 60 percent. Failing either test is enough — unless the employee actually enrolls, when § 36B(c)(2)(C)(iii) disapplies both.

drills.prompt: A family's expected contribution is $300 a month, the second lowest cost silver plan costs $980, and they buy a bronze plan for $520. What is the monthly credit?
drills.answer: $520. Section 36B(b)(2)(B) gives $980 less $300, or $680, but § 36B(b)(2)(A) caps the premium assistance amount at the premiums actually paid for the plans they enrolled in. The bronze plan therefore costs them nothing and the excess benchmark credit is not paid to them.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer whose income is below the filing threshold received advance payments all year. Must they file?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 36B(f)(1) and (2) require the credit to be reconciled against the advance payments, which can only happen on a return. Filing is required regardless of the income threshold and regardless of whether the reconciliation produces a refund or a balance.

drills.prompt: In which month does eligibility for Medicare end the credit — the month of enrolment or the month of eligibility?
drills.answer: Eligibility. Section 36B(c)(2)(B)(i) excludes from coverage months any month for which the individual is eligible for minimum essential coverage other than individual market coverage, and Medicare is minimum essential coverage under § 5000A(f). Declining to enrol does not preserve the credit.

drills.prompt: A married couple file jointly with adjusted gross income of $41,000. She contributed $3,000 to a 401(k) and he contributed $1,200 to a Roth IRA. What is the saver's credit for 2026?
drills.answer: $2,000 is not right, and neither is 20 percent of anything. At $41,000 they are in the 50 percent band for a joint return. Her contributions are capped at $2,000 by IRC § 25B(a) and his are $1,200, so the base is $3,200 and the credit is $1,600, assuming no testing period distributions.

drills.prompt: An employee worked for one employer all year and had social security tax withheld above the wage base. How is it recovered?
drills.answer: From the employer, not on the return. IRC § 6413(c)(1) gives a special refund only where the employee received wages from more than one employer, so no § 31(b) credit arises. The employer must refund the excess and furnish a corrected Form W-2.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer paid for and completed a residential solar installation in March 2026. What credit is available under § 25D?
drills.answer: None. Section 25D(h) provides that the credit does not apply to expenditures made after 31 December 2025, following the amendment by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70506. The date of the contract is irrelevant.

drills.prompt: A 61-year-old receiving Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation payments asks about the health coverage tax credit. What is the answer?
drills.answer: It is no longer available. IRC § 35(b)(1)(B) requires an eligible coverage month to begin before 1 January 2022, so no credit has been available since taxable year 2021, whatever the taxpayer's age or source of assistance.

drills.prompt: Why does a taxpayer aged 70 with $22,000 of social security and a $4,000 pension get no credit under § 22?
drills.answer: Because the § 22(c)(2)(A) initial amount for a single individual is $5,000 and § 22(c)(3) reduces it by nontaxable social security. Benefits of $22,000 exceed the initial amount several times over, so the section 22 amount is zero before the § 22(d) adjusted gross income reduction is even reached. The figures have not been indexed since 1983.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer has a minimum tax credit carryforward of $1,200, regular tax liability of $2,500 and tentative minimum tax of $2,000, with no other nonrefundable credits. How much carries to the next year?
drills.answer: $700. IRC § 53(c) limits the credit to regular tax liability reduced by other allowable credits, less the tentative minimum tax — $500 here. The unused $700 remains in the § 53(b) carryforward, which has no expiry.
drills.pageTitle: Alternative minimum tax and credit for prior year

drills.prompt: Which of a property tax deduction, a state income tax deduction, a depreciation adjustment and mortgage interest can produce a credit under § 53?
drills.answer: The depreciation adjustment. It is a deferral item — the deduction is taken in a different year under each system, so the difference reverses. The two tax deductions are exclusion items under § 56(b)(1)(A)(ii), permanently disallowed, and § 53(d)(1)(B) removes exclusion preferences from the adjusted net minimum tax.
drills.pageTitle: Alternative minimum tax and credit for prior year

drills.prompt: A joint return shows alternative minimum taxable income of $1,100,000 for 2026. By how much is the exemption reduced?
drills.answer: By $50,000. Income exceeds the $1,000,000 threshold by $100,000, and IRC § 55(d)(4)(A)(ii)(IV) sets the reduction at 50 percent of the excess for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025. Under the former 25 percent rate the reduction would have been $25,000.
drills.pageTitle: Alternative minimum tax and credit for prior year

drills.prompt: An employee exercises incentive stock options in November and holds the shares into the following year. What happens for alternative minimum tax purposes?
drills.answer: The spread between the exercise price and the fair market value at exercise is included in alternative minimum taxable income for the year of exercise, because IRC § 56(b)(3) disapplies § 421 for this purpose. Any resulting minimum tax is a deferral item and generates a § 53 credit.
drills.pageTitle: Alternative minimum tax and credit for prior year

drills.prompt: Is a taxpayer with tax-exempt interest from a municipal bond issued to build a public school affected by § 57(a)(5)?
drills.answer: Only if it is a specified private activity bond. Section 57(a)(5)(A) makes interest on such bonds a preference item; ordinary governmental purpose bonds are not within it. A mutual fund's exempt-interest dividend carries the preference through to the shareholder in proportion to the fund's private activity bond interest under § 57(a)(5)(B).
drills.pageTitle: Alternative minimum tax and credit for prior year

drills.prompt: A family pays a housekeeper $3,050 in cash wages in 2026. On how much is social security and Medicare tax due?
drills.answer: On the whole $3,050. IRC § 3121(a)(7)(B) excludes the cash remuneration only where it is *less than* the applicable dollar threshold for the year. Once the wages equal or exceed the threshold the exclusion does not apply at all, so every dollar is taxed, not merely the excess.

drills.prompt: Which taxes must a household employer withhold from an employee's wages?
drills.answer: Social security and Medicare, once the cash wage threshold is met, plus the additional Medicare tax on wages above its own threshold. Federal income tax is withheld only if the employer and employee agree, under IRC § 3402(p). Federal unemployment tax is never withheld — the employer pays it from their own funds.

drills.prompt: A couple pay their 19-year-old daughter $5,000 to look after her younger siblings. What are the employment tax consequences?
drills.answer: None of the household employment taxes apply. A child under the age of 21 is excluded from social security and Medicare withholding, and wages paid to a child under 21 are excluded from the FUTA tests as well. The daughter still has taxable income to report.

drills.prompt: A family paid a gardener $700 in each of the four quarters of the prior year and $900 in the first quarter of this year. Is federal unemployment tax due this year?
drills.answer: No, on these facts. FUTA applies where cash wages to household employees exceeded $1,000 in any calendar quarter of the current or prior year, and no quarter in either year did. Note that the test is aggregate across household employees, so another worker paid in the same quarter could change the answer.

drills.prompt: A household employer is not required to file an income tax return. How are the household employment taxes reported?
drills.answer: On Schedule H filed by itself. IRC § 3510 coordinates the collection of domestic service employment taxes with the income tax by putting them on the individual return, and where there is no return to attach it to, the schedule stands alone.

drills.prompt: Last year a taxpayer's adjusted gross income was $180,000 and their tax was $40,000. What estimated payments defeat the § 6654 addition this year regardless of this year's liability?
drills.answer: $44,000, paid in four equal instalments of $11,000 by the four due dates. Because prior year adjusted gross income exceeded the § 6654(d)(1)(C)(i) threshold, the prior-year leg of the required annual payment is 110 percent rather than 100 percent.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer's tax for the year, after withholding, is $850. They made no estimated payments. Is there an addition to tax?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 6654(e)(1) imposes no addition where the tax shown on the return, reduced by the § 31 credit for withheld tax, is less than $1,000. The exception is tested after withholding, not on gross liability.

drills.prompt: Why does a taxpayer who pays the entire year's tax with the fourth instalment still owe an addition?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 6654(b) computes the underpayment and its period instalment by instalment. The first three required instalments were unpaid from their own due dates, and the addition runs on each for the days it remained short. Only the annualised income method under § 6654(d)(2), or withholding, can reach back to those quarters.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer files five months late and pays at the same time. What is the failure to file addition on $6,000 of tax?
drills.answer: $1,350. The addition is 5 percent a month capped at 25 percent — five months gives 25 percent, or $1,500 — reduced under IRC § 6651(c)(1) by the failure to pay addition of 0.5 percent for five months, or $150. Both remain subject to the reasonable cause defence.

drills.prompt: Does reasonable cause abate the interest charged under § 6601?
drills.answer: No. Section 6601 charges interest at the § 6621 underpayment rate for the period the tax is unpaid, and it is not an addition to tax subject to a reasonable cause defence. Reasonable cause reaches the § 6651 additions and the § 6654 addition through its own waiver provisions, but the interest runs regardless.

drills.prompt: A collector who has owned stamps for years sells a single rare item at a large gain. Is the gain subject to self-employment tax?
drills.answer: No. Self-employment tax reaches net earnings from a trade or business carried on by the taxpayer, and IRC § 1402(a)(3) excludes gain from the disposition of property that is not stock in trade or held primarily for sale to customers. An isolated sale by a collector does not establish a trade or business, so the gain is a capital gain.
drills.pageTitle: Self-employment tax: who owes it and the optional methods

drills.prompt: Why would a taxpayer elect an optional method that increases their self-employment tax?
drills.answer: For social security quarters of coverage, and because the earned income credit and the additional child tax credit are computed on earned income. Raising reported net earnings can increase those credits by more than the additional tax costs, which is why the election exists at all.
drills.pageTitle: Self-employment tax: who owes it and the optional methods

drills.prompt: A taxpayer used the non-farm optional method in each of the last five years. May they use it again?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 1402(a) limits the non-farm optional method to five taxable years for any individual. The farm optional method has no such limit, so a taxpayer with farm income could continue to use that one.
drills.pageTitle: Self-employment tax: who owes it and the optional methods

drills.prompt: A minister filed an approved exemption application under § 1402(e) and now also earns fees from an unrelated consulting business. What is the position?
drills.answer: The exemption covers services performed as a minister and does not reach the consulting fees, which are self-employment income in the ordinary way. The exemption is also irrevocable, so it cannot be withdrawn to obtain coverage.
drills.pageTitle: Self-employment tax: who owes it and the optional methods

drills.prompt: A self-employed taxpayer has enough itemized deductions to reduce income tax to zero and holds a nonrefundable credit. What does the credit do to the self-employment tax?
drills.answer: Nothing. Sections 1401(a) and (b) impose the tax in chapter 2, and IRC § 26(a) limits nonrefundable credits to the chapter 1 liability. The self-employment tax is payable in full and can only be met by payments or refundable credits.
drills.pageTitle: Self-employment tax: who owes it and the optional methods

drills.prompt: A taxpayer with two employers had a total of $12,900 of social security tax withheld for 2026. What is the credit?
drills.answer: The excess over 6.2 percent of the contribution and benefit base for the year — $12,900 less $11,439, or $1,461. IRC § 6413(c)(1) gives the special refund and § 31(b)(1) treats it as an amount withheld at source, so it is recovered whatever the taxpayer's liability.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer with one employer had social security tax withheld on wages above the base. May they claim a credit?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 6413(c)(1) applies only where the excess arises "by reason of an employee receiving wages from more than one employer". The employer must refund the over-withheld amount and issue a corrected Form W-2; if it refuses, the employee claims on Form 843 with a statement to that effect.

drills.prompt: Does Medicare tax withheld above any threshold generate a similar credit?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 3101(b)(1) imposes the hospital insurance tax on all covered wages with no ceiling, so there is no excess to recover. The separate 0.9 percent additional Medicare tax under § 3101(b)(2) is reconciled on the taxpayer's own return on Form 8959, which can produce either a balance due or a credit.

drills.prompt: A married couple file jointly. One spouse's wages were well below the base and the other's, from two employers, well above. Can the couple net the two?
drills.answer: No. The contribution and benefit base applies to each individual's own wages, so the spouse with two employers computes the excess on their own figures and the other spouse's unused base is irrelevant. The two amounts are computed separately and then reported on the joint return.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer worked for two different federal agencies during the year. Is that two employers for this purpose?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 6413(c)(2)(A) deems each head of a federal agency or instrumentality who makes a return under § 3122, and each designated agent who does so, to be a separate employer for the purposes of the special refund.

drills.prompt: A minister receives $40,000 of salary, $3,000 of fees, and lives in a church-owned home with a fair rental value of $12,000. What are the income tax and self-employment tax bases?
drills.answer: $43,000 for income tax, because IRC § 107(1) excludes the rental value of a home furnished as part of compensation. $55,000 for self-employment tax, because § 1402(a)(8) requires net earnings from ministerial service to be computed without regard to § 107.
drills.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the clergy

drills.prompt: A church designates a housing allowance in June for salary paid from January. How much of the January to May salary is excludable?
drills.answer: None of it. Reg. § 1.107-1(b) requires the designation to be by official action taken in advance of the payment. The designation is effective only for payments made after it is adopted.
drills.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the clergy

drills.prompt: Which of a vow of poverty, a vow of obedience, and conscientious opposition to public insurance exempts a minister from self-employment tax?
drills.answer: The vow of poverty, for a member of a religious order, and the conscientious or religious opposition, on an approved application under IRC § 1402(e). A vow of obedience is not among them. The closing sentence of § 1402(c) carves out the vow of poverty; everyone else needs the application.
drills.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the clergy

drills.prompt: A minister excludes a $20,000 housing allowance and uses it to pay mortgage interest and property taxes. May those amounts still be deducted?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 265(a) would ordinarily deny a deduction allocable to tax-exempt income, but § 265(a)(6)(B) provides that no deduction is denied for mortgage interest or real property taxes on the taxpayer's home by reason of receiving a parsonage allowance excludable under § 107.
drills.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the clergy

drills.prompt: A retired minister's former denomination designates part of a church plan pension as a housing allowance. What is the treatment?
drills.answer: Excluded from gross income under IRC § 107 to the extent of the usual limits, and also outside net earnings from self-employment — § 1402(a)(8) expressly removes a parsonage allowance provided after retirement and any other church plan retirement benefit from the self-employment tax base.
drills.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the clergy

drills.prompt: An enlisted member serves in a designated combat zone from 27 June to 4 July. How much compensation is excluded?
drills.answer: All of June's and all of July's. IRC § 112(a) excludes compensation for active service for any month "during any part of which" the member served in a combat zone, so both months are excluded in full with no proration for the days actually served.
drills.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the military

drills.prompt: Does a commissioned officer exclude combat zone pay without limit?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 112(b) limits the exclusion to the maximum enlisted amount — the highest basic pay for an enlisted member at the highest pay grade for that month, plus hostile fire or imminent danger pay where the officer receives it. A commissioned warrant officer is outside this limit by § 112(c)(1).
drills.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the military

drills.prompt: A member is hospitalised in the United States for wounds received in a combat zone. Is the pay still excluded?
drills.answer: Yes, for months of continuous hospitalisation attributable to the wounds, but not for a month beginning more than two years after combatant activities in that zone terminate (IRC § 112(a)(2), (b)(2)). The same hospitalisation period also extends the § 7508 suspension of deadlines.
drills.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the military

drills.prompt: May a civilian employee who moves for a new job deduct the cost?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 217(k)(1) suspends the deduction for taxable years beginning after 2017 and Pub. L. 119-21 § 70113(a) made that permanent. Two classes survive: a member of the Armed Forces moving under orders on a permanent change of station (§ 217(g)), and from 2026 an employee or new appointee of the intelligence community relocating on assignment (§ 217(k)(2)).
drills.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the military

drills.prompt: A service member deployed for six years sells the home they lived in before deploying. Can the § 121 exclusion still apply?
drills.answer: Yes, if they elect under IRC § 121(d)(9)(A) to suspend the running of the five-year period during the qualified official extended duty. The suspension is capped at ten years by § 121(d)(9)(B), and it is an election rather than an automatic rule.
drills.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the military

drills.prompt: A taxpayer sold shares held for ten years at a gain and died before the proceeds were received. The beneficiary collects them. What is the character of the income?
drills.answer: Long-term capital gain. IRC § 691(a)(3) treats the right in the recipient's hands as if acquired in the transaction in which the right to the income was originally derived, so both the character and the decedent's holding period carry across.

drills.prompt: Why is an inherited traditional individual retirement account taxable when an inherited brokerage account is not?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 1014(c) excludes property constituting a right to receive an item of income in respect of a decedent from the date-of-death basis rule. The retirement account is such a right, so it takes no step-up and the taxable portion is income under § 691(a) when received; the brokerage account takes a § 1014(a) basis and the pre-death appreciation is never taxed.

drills.prompt: An estate sells a right to future income with a fair market value of $50,000 for $44,000. What does it include?
drills.answer: $50,000. IRC § 691(a)(2) includes the fair market value of the right at the time of transfer, plus the amount by which any consideration exceeds that value. A sale below value does not reduce the inclusion.

drills.prompt: Does the § 691(c) deduction survive the disallowance of miscellaneous itemized deductions?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 67(b)(7) excludes the deduction under § 691(c) from the definition of a miscellaneous itemized deduction, so the § 67(h) disallowance does not reach it. It remains an itemized deduction, so it is available only to a taxpayer who itemizes.

drills.prompt: A decedent's final medical practice expenses are paid by the residuary beneficiary who took the practice subject to them, the estate having no liability. Who deducts them?
drills.answer: The beneficiary. IRC § 691(b)(1)(B) allows the deduction to the person who, by reason of the death or by bequest, devise or inheritance, acquires from the decedent an interest in property subject to the obligation, where the estate is not liable to discharge it. The deduction is allowed in the taxable year when paid.

drills.prompt: A single taxpayer has $190,000 of wages and $22,000 of net investment income. What is the tax?
drills.answer: $456. Net investment income is $22,000 and modified adjusted gross income exceeds the $200,000 threshold by $12,000, so IRC § 1411(a)(1) applies 3.8 percent to the lesser figure of $12,000.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer with $600,000 of modified adjusted gross income takes a $150,000 distribution from a traditional individual retirement account. Is it subject to the tax?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 1411(c)(5) excludes any distribution from a plan or arrangement described in §§ 401(a), 403(a), 403(b), 408, 408A or 457(b) from net investment income. The distribution does, however, increase modified adjusted gross income and so can expose other investment income to the tax.

drills.prompt: Why is a sole proprietor's business profit not subject to the net investment income tax?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 1411(c)(6) excludes any item taken into account in determining self-employment income on which the § 1401(b) tax is imposed. The profit bears the hospital insurance component of self-employment tax instead, and the same dollar is never subject to both.

drills.prompt: Two taxpayers each have $40,000 of rental income and identical high incomes. Why might only one owe the tax?
drills.answer: Because § 1411(c)(2)(A) brings in a trade or business that is a passive activity within § 469. Where the taxpayer materially participates, the rents are derived in the ordinary course of a trade or business not described in that paragraph and are excluded by § 1411(c)(1)(A)(i); where they do not, the income is caught in full.

drills.prompt: Is the threshold adjusted for inflation?
drills.answer: No. The amounts in IRC § 1411(b) are fixed in the statute with no indexing provision, and have been unchanged since the tax took effect for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2012. Only the estate and trust threshold moves, because § 1411(a)(2)(B)(ii) points at the indexed start of the highest § 1(e) bracket.

drills.prompt: A single taxpayer has $185,000 of wages and $35,000 of self-employment income. What is the additional Medicare tax?
drills.answer: $180. The threshold applies to the combined $220,000, giving an excess of $20,000 taxed at 0.9 percent. Neither source alone crosses the threshold, and the employer withholds nothing because the wages are below the § 3102(f)(1) trigger.

drills.prompt: A married couple filing jointly earn $210,000 and $65,000. The higher earner's employer withheld the tax on wages above $200,000. What is payable with the return?
drills.answer: $135. Combined wages of $275,000 exceed the $250,000 joint threshold by $25,000, giving a liability of $225. The employer withheld 0.9 percent of $10,000, or $90, which is credited, leaving $135.

drills.prompt: Two employers each pay a single taxpayer $150,000. How much do they withhold?
drills.answer: Nothing. IRC § 3102(f)(1) requires withholding only to the extent the taxpayer receives wages from that employer in excess of $200,000, and expressly permits the employer to disregard other wages. The taxpayer owes 0.9 percent of $100,000 at filing.

drills.prompt: Does the additional Medicare tax on self-employment income enter the deduction for one half of self-employment tax?
drills.answer: No. The § 1401(b)(2) tax is disregarded both in the § 1402(a)(12) reduction of net earnings and in the § 164(f) deduction for one half of the tax. It is the only component of self-employment tax that receives neither halving.

drills.prompt: A married taxpayer files separately with $210,000 of wages. Is the employer's withholding enough?
drills.answer: No. The employer withholds on the $10,000 above $200,000, but the threshold for a married individual filing separately is $125,000 — half the joint figure — so the liability is 0.9 percent of $85,000. The difference is settled on Form 8959.

drills.prompt: A Form W-2 shows $310 in box 12 with code A. How is it treated?
drills.answer: As an addition to tax. Code A is uncollected social security tax on tips — the employee's share that the employer could not collect under IRC § 3102(c)(1) — and it is added to the individual's liability, not credited as withholding.
drills.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

drills.prompt: An employee receives $18 of cash tips in one month and $140 in the next. What is reportable?
drills.answer: Only the second month's. IRC § 3121(a)(12)(B) excludes cash tips received in a calendar month from wages unless they amount to $20 or more, so the $18 month is outside the employment tax system entirely — though the income tax on it is still due.
drills.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

drills.prompt: Why can an employer be unable to collect the tax on properly reported tips?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 3102(c)(1) permits collection only from wages of the employee excluding tips that are under the employer's control, and only within the period ending on the tenth day of the month following the month the tips were deemed paid. A tipped worker with little or no hourly pay leaves nothing to collect from.
drills.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

drills.prompt: What is the consequence of not reporting tips to the employer at all?
drills.answer: The employee owes the employee share of social security and Medicare tax on them directly, computed on Form 4137, and is liable under IRC § 6652(b) for an additional 50 percent of that tax unless the failure was due to reasonable cause and not wilful neglect.
drills.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

drills.prompt: Does the new deduction for qualified tips remove them from social security and Medicare tax?
drills.answer: No. The IRC § 224 deduction operates in computing taxable income only. Tips remain wages under § 3121(a) and (q), the § 6053(a) reporting obligation is unchanged, and the employee share of FICA is due on the same dollars.
drills.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

drills.prompt: A taxpayer claimed the 2008 first-time homebuyer credit. How is it repaid?
drills.answer: In equal annual instalments of 6⅔ percent of the credit across a 15-year recapture period beginning with the second taxable year after the year of purchase — $500 a year on the maximum $7,500 credit (IRC § 36(f)(1), (7)).

drills.prompt: The same taxpayer sells the home to an unrelated buyer at a loss before the period ends. What is owed?
drills.answer: Nothing further. IRC § 36(f)(2) accelerates the unrecaptured balance into the year of disposition, but § 36(f)(3) limits the increase to the gain on a sale to an unrelated person, and there is no gain. Section 36(f)(2)(B) then switches off the annual instalments for that year and after.

drills.prompt: An excess individual retirement account contribution is left in place for four years. How many times is the § 4973 tax imposed?
drills.answer: Four. The tax is 6 percent of the excess determined as of the close of each taxable year, so it recurs for every year the excess remains in the account, capped at 6 percent of the account value.

drills.prompt: Does a taxpayer with no income tax liability owe the tax on a missed required minimum distribution?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 4974(a) imposes the tax on the payee at 25 percent of the shortfall regardless of income tax liability, and nonrefundable credits do not reduce it.

drills.prompt: What is the shared responsibility payment for 2026?
drills.answer: Zero. IRC § 5000A(a) and (b) still state the requirement and the penalty, but § 5000A(c)(2)(B)(iii) sets the percentage of income at zero for taxable years beginning after 2018 and § 5000A(c)(3)(A) sets the applicable dollar amount at $0, so the monthly penalty amount is the greater of two zeros.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer receives $12,000 across 300 transactions through an online payment platform in 2026. Will a Form 1099-K be issued?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 6050W(e) as restored by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70432 requires both the dollar amount and the transaction count to be exceeded. The count is met and the amount is not, so no return is required. The income, if any, is reportable regardless.

drills.prompt: A business pays an unincorporated contractor $1,500 during 2026. Is an information return required?
drills.answer: No. The IRC § 6041(a) threshold for payments made after 31 December 2025 exceeds that amount, following Pub. L. 119-21 § 70433(a), so no return is required. The contractor's income is taxable all the same.

drills.prompt: A dealer receives $6,500 in cash on one day and $4,800 in cash a week later for the same vehicle. What is required?
drills.answer: A Form 8300. IRC § 6050I(a) applies where more than $10,000 in cash is received in one transaction or two or more related transactions, and payments for a single vehicle are related. The aggregate of $11,300 exceeds the threshold.

drills.prompt: Two professionals exchange services of equal value with no barter exchange involved. What are the consequences?
drills.answer: Each has gross income equal to the fair market value of what they received under IRC § 61(a), and each may have a deductible business expense of the same amount. No information return is required, because neither is a barter exchange within § 6045(c)(3), and the absence of a form does not affect taxability.

drills.prompt: A payer files 100 incorrect information returns through intentional disregard. What is the exposure?
drills.answer: Under IRC § 6721(e)(2)(A) the penalty is the greater of $690 per return or 10 percent of the aggregate amount required to be reported correctly, with no calendar year maximum — and a parallel penalty applies under § 6722 for the corresponding payee statements.

drills.prompt: Which of a copyright, a vehicle, land and a collectible is not personal property?
drills.answer: Land. Personal property is all property other than real property, and real property is land and what is permanently affixed to it. A copyright, a vehicle and a collectible are all personal property, though they are taxed very differently from one another on sale.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer sells a coin collection held for six years at a $40,000 gain. What rate applies?
drills.answer: 28 percent, as 28-percent rate gain. Coins are collectibles within IRC § 408(m) as applied by § 1(h)(5)(A), and § 1(h)(4) combines collectibles gain with § 1202 gain into a category taxed at a maximum of 28 percent — reduced by collectibles losses, net short-term capital loss and long-term capital loss carried forward.

drills.prompt: A rental property is sold at a gain after $85,000 of straight-line depreciation. How is that $85,000 taxed?
drills.answer: As unrecaptured section 1250 gain, at a maximum rate of 25 percent under IRC § 1(h)(1)(E) and (6). It is not ordinary income — that is § 1245 recapture, which applies to personal property — and it is not eligible for the zero, 15 or 20 percent rates.

drills.prompt: Does selling a partnership interest instead of the underlying artwork change the rate?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 1(h)(5)(B) treats gain on the sale of an interest in a partnership, S corporation or trust attributable to unrealised appreciation in collectibles as collectibles gain, applying rules similar to § 751. The 28 percent rate follows the underlying asset.

drills.prompt: A single taxpayer with $42,000 of other taxable income realises a $30,000 long-term gain. Is the whole gain taxed at zero?
drills.answer: No. The zero rate applies only to so much of the adjusted net capital gain as fits below the maximum zero rate amount for the filing status, measured by taxable income. The gain itself lifts the taxpayer past that ceiling, and the excess is taxed at 15 percent.

drills.prompt: What is the maximum § 529 distribution for elementary and secondary expenses in 2026?
drills.answer: $20,000 per beneficiary for the year. Pub. L. 119-21 § 70413(b) doubled the previous $10,000 figure for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025. Any source giving $10,000 is describing 2025 and earlier.

drills.prompt: May a § 529 account pay for private tutoring?
drills.answer: Yes, within limits. IRC § 529(c)(7)(E) covers tuition for tutoring or educational classes outside the home where the tutor is not related to the student and is either licensed as a teacher in any State, has taught at an eligible educational institution, or is a subject matter expert in the relevant subject.

drills.prompt: A client's son is in a recognised electrician credential programme. Can the § 529 account pay the testing fee for the licence?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 529(f)(1)(B) treats fees for testing required to obtain or maintain a recognised postsecondary credential as qualified postsecondary credentialing expenses, which § 529(e)(3)(C) brings within qualified higher education expenses.

drills.prompt: Can an employer permanently exclude payments toward an employee's student loans?
drills.answer: Yes. Pub. L. 119-21 § 70412(a) struck the 1 January 2026 cut-off from IRC § 127(c)(1)(B), so employer payments of principal or interest on a qualified education loan remain within the exclusion indefinitely, subject to the annual limit — which § 127(d) now indexes from 2027.

drills.prompt: A family pays $12,000 of tuition entirely from a § 529 distribution and claims an education credit on it. What is wrong?
drills.answer: The same expenses cannot support both a tax-free qualified tuition program distribution and an education credit. Allocating part of the tuition to other funds preserves the credit while still using the account for the balance.

drills.prompt: A client gives appreciated shares to a child instead of leaving them by will. What is the income tax consequence?
drills.answer: The child takes the donor's basis under IRC § 1015(a), so the whole appreciation remains taxable on a later sale. Had the shares passed at death, § 1014(a) would have given a basis equal to fair market value at death and the appreciation would never have been taxed.

drills.prompt: An estate passes entirely to a surviving spouse and owes no estate tax. Is a return needed?
drills.answer: Yes, if portability is wanted. IRC § 2010(c)(5)(A) makes the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount available only where the first estate filed a timely and complete estate tax return electing it. The tax owed is irrelevant to that requirement.

drills.prompt: Are life insurance proceeds taxable?
drills.answer: Not for income tax — IRC § 101(a)(1) excludes amounts paid by reason of the insured's death. But § 2042 includes them in the gross estate if receivable by the executor, or if the decedent possessed any incident of ownership at death. The two systems reach opposite answers on the same money.

drills.prompt: How many donees can receive an annual exclusion gift?
drills.answer: Any number. The IRC § 2503(b) exclusion applies per donee per calendar year with no limit on the number of donees, provided each gift is of a present interest rather than a future interest.

drills.prompt: Does the basic exclusion amount fall back after 2025?
drills.answer: No. Pub. L. 119-21 § 70106 amended IRC § 2010(c)(3) to set a new amount for calendar year 2026, indexed from calendar year 2025 for decedents dying after 2026. The scheduled reduction that drove much 2018–2025 planning no longer applies.

drills.prompt: A nephew inherits a traditional IRA. Which option is unavailable to him?
drills.answer: Rolling the balance into an IRA of his own. Only a surviving spouse may treat an inherited account as their own or roll it over; a non-spouse beneficiary must take it as an inherited account under the IRC § 401(a)(9)(B) distribution rules. A lump sum, distributions over a period, or an annuity where available are all possible.

drills.prompt: A 74-year-old still working for an unrelated employer owns 2 percent of it. When must distributions from the employer plan begin?
drills.answer: Not until 1 April of the year following retirement. IRC § 401(a)(9)(C)(i) uses the later of the applicable age and retirement, and the § 401(a)(9)(C)(ii) exception for 5-percent owners does not reach a 2 percent holding. Any IRA of theirs is a different matter — the retirement limb never applies to one.

drills.prompt: Why is a qualified charitable distribution better than writing a cheque for a client who does not itemise?
drills.answer: Because it is an exclusion from gross income under IRC § 408(d)(8)(A) rather than a deduction. The amount never enters adjusted gross income, so the benefit is available regardless of the standard deduction, and the lower adjusted gross income can reduce the taxable portion of social security and other income-linked amounts. It also counts toward the required distribution.

drills.prompt: A client aged 72 has deducted IRA contributions since turning 70½. Does that affect a qualified charitable distribution?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 408(d)(8)(A) reduces the excludable amount by the aggregate deductions allowed under § 219 for all taxable years ending on or after the individual attained age 70½, less reductions already applied in earlier years. The offset is cumulative and does not reset.

drills.prompt: A single taxpayer with no workplace retirement plan and adjusted gross income of $200,000 wants to deduct an IRA contribution. Can they?
drills.answer: Yes, in full. The IRC § 219(g) phase-out applies only to an active participant in an employer plan. With no such plan and no spouse who is a participant, there is no income limit on the deduction.

drills.prompt: A couple divorce on 5 December. What filing status is available for that year?
drills.answer: Single, or head of household if its separate conditions are met. IRC § 7703(a)(1) determines marital status as of the close of the taxable year, so a decree entered in December makes both parties unmarried for the whole year regardless of how long they were married during it.

drills.prompt: A 2015 divorce decree requires alimony. Is a payment made in 2026 deductible?
drills.answer: Yes. Pub. L. 115-97 § 11051 repealed IRC §§ 71 and 215 only for instruments executed after 31 December 2018. A pre-2019 instrument keeps the deduction and the corresponding inclusion, unless it has been modified after 2018 with an express provision that the repeal applies.

drills.prompt: One spouse takes a house with a low basis and the other an account of equal value with a high basis. Is the division tax-neutral?
drills.answer: Not economically. IRC § 1041(a) means neither recognises gain on the transfer, but § 1041(b)(2) gives each the transferor's adjusted basis, so the spouse taking the low-basis asset carries the larger unrealised gain. Equal value is not equal after tax.

drills.prompt: A married taxpayer files separately and lived with their spouse for part of the year. What is the base amount for taxing social security benefits?
drills.answer: Zero. IRC § 86(c)(1)(C) sets the base amount at zero for a taxpayer who is married at the close of the year, does not file a joint return, and does not live apart from their spouse at all times during the year. Benefits are taxable from the first dollar of other income.

drills.prompt: Does a divorce decree assigning the tax liability to one spouse protect the other from the IRS?
drills.answer: No. A joint return creates joint and several liability under IRC § 6013(d)(3), and a decree binds the spouses rather than the Service. The only relief runs through § 6015, on its own conditions and deadlines.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer carries forward a $2,500 long-term capital loss into a year with a $1,500 long-term gain and a $3,000 short-term gain. What is the result?
drills.answer: A $2,000 net short-term gain. Under IRC § 1212(b)(1)(B) the carryover retains its long-term character, offsets the long-term gain first, and the remaining $1,000 then reduces the short-term gain.
drills.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

drills.prompt: Which is not a component of the general business credit — the investment credit, the minimum tax credit, the work opportunity credit or the energy efficient home credit?
drills.answer: The minimum tax credit. It is allowed under IRC § 53 as a credit for prior year minimum tax liability and is not among the credits aggregated into the general business credit under § 38.
drills.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

drills.prompt: How long may an individual carry forward a charitable contribution that exceeded the percentage limitation?
drills.answer: Five succeeding taxable years, in order of time, under IRC § 170(d)(1)(A). In each of those years it is used after the current year's contributions and remains subject to the applicable percentage limitation.
drills.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

drills.prompt: A client has net operating losses from 2016 and 2022. Which is used first?
drills.answer: The 2016 loss. IRC § 172(a)(2)(A) allows losses arising in taxable years beginning before 1 January 2018 in full and before the post-2017 pool, which is separately limited to 80 percent of taxable income computed without the § 172, § 199A and § 250 deductions.
drills.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

drills.prompt: A business has a qualified business income loss this year and profits next year. What happens?
drills.answer: IRC § 199A(c)(2) treats the negative net amount as a loss from a qualified trade or business in the succeeding taxable year, reducing next year's qualified business income and therefore the deduction. Nothing on the loss year's return records it, so it has to be tracked deliberately.
drills.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

drills.prompt: A couple's joint refund is taken to pay one spouse's pre-marital defaulted federal student loan. What is the remedy?
drills.answer: An injured spouse allocation on Form 8379. The debt is a past-due legally enforceable debt owed to a federal agency within IRC § 6402(d), and the non-debtor spouse claims the portion of the joint overpayment attributable to their own income, withholding and credits.

drills.prompt: The same couple's refund is instead applied to their own joint balance from a prior year. Does Form 8379 help?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 6402(a) credits an overpayment against a liability of the person who made it, and a joint return makes that liability joint and several under § 6013(d)(3). The debt is the claimant's own, so there is no injured spouse claim — relief, if any, would have to come under § 6015.

drills.prompt: Who notifies the taxpayer of an offset, and who should they contact?
drills.answer: The Bureau of the Fiscal Service, which administers the Treasury Offset Program, sends a notice showing the original refund, the offset and the agency paid. The details are not provided to the IRS, so the taxpayer should contact the Bureau unless the refund amount on the notice differs from the amount on the return.

drills.prompt: Why might an injured spouse in a community property state recover less?
drills.answer: Because community income and the withholding on it are generally treated as belonging half to each spouse under state law, which the Service applies to the allocation. A larger share of the overpayment is therefore attributable to the debtor spouse than the same facts would produce in a common law state.

drills.prompt: When is the best time to file the allocation?
drills.answer: With the original return, where the couple already knows an offset is likely. That prevents the offset rather than reversing it and avoids the months a post-offset claim takes to work.

drills.prompt: A couple filed accurately, owe $30,000 they never paid, and have since separated. Which route is available?
drills.answer: Equitable relief under IRC § 6015(f) only. Subsections (b) and (c) require an understatement or a deficiency, and there is neither — the liability was correctly reported. The request must be made before the § 6502 collection period expires.

drills.prompt: A divorced taxpayer elects allocation under § 6015(c) after paying part of the deficiency. What happens to the payment?
drills.answer: Nothing. IRC § 6015(g)(3) allows no credit or refund as a result of a § 6015(c) election. To recover an amount already paid the request has to rest on § 6015(b) or § 6015(f), subject to the § 6511 refund claim period.

drills.prompt: When does the two-year period for a § 6015(b) election begin?
drills.answer: On the date the Secretary began collection activities with respect to the individual making the election (IRC § 6015(b)(1)(E)) — not on assessment, not on filing, and not on divorce.

drills.prompt: A requesting spouse knew of part of an understatement but not its size. What relief is available under § 6015(b)?
drills.answer: Partial. IRC § 6015(b)(2) relieves the individual of liability to the extent attributable to the portion of the understatement of which they did not know and had no reason to know, provided the other conditions are met.

drills.prompt: Six months after filing a request, the Service has not determined it. What can the taxpayer do?
drills.answer: Petition the Tax Court. IRC § 6015(e)(1)(A)(i)(II) allows a petition at any time after the date six months after the election or request, without waiting for a final determination notice; where such a notice is issued, the petition must be filed within 90 days of it.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer's preceding year showed tax of $30,000 and adjusted gross income of $190,000. Her current-year tax is $26,000. What is her required annual payment?
drills.answer: $33,000. Because the preceding year's adjusted gross income exceeded $150,000, IRC § 6654(d)(1)(C)(i) substitutes 110 percent for 100 percent, giving $33,000 on the prior-year branch. The current-year branch is 90 percent of $26,000, or $23,400, and the required annual payment is the lesser of the two — but the taxpayer must know the current year's tax to rely on it, which she does not until the year ends.
drills.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

drills.prompt: A client with no estimated tax payments increases his withholding sharply in December, ending the year with total withholding equal to his prior-year tax. Has he underpaid any installment?
drills.answer: No. Under IRC § 6654(g)(1) the credit allowed under § 31 is deemed a payment of estimated tax paid in equal parts on each due date, unless the taxpayer establishes the actual dates. The December withholding is treated as one quarter paid in April, one in June, one in September and one in January.
drills.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer files her return and pays the balance in full on 28 January. Which installments does that protect?
drills.answer: The fourth only. IRC § 6654(h) removes the addition with respect to an underpayment of the fourth required installment where the return is filed and paid in full on or before 31 January. Any shortfall in the first three installments is unaffected.
drills.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

drills.prompt: A farmer's gross income from farming is 70 percent of his total gross income. How many installments must he make, and when?
drills.answer: One, due 15 January of the following year. IRC § 6654(i)(1) allows a single required installment for a farmer or fisherman — defined in § 6654(i)(2) as one whose farming or fishing gross income is at least 66⅔ percent of gross income from all sources for the year or the preceding year — computed by substituting 66⅔ percent for 90 percent and disregarding the 110 percent rule.
drills.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer annualises and pays nothing for the first installment. What happens to the amount he did not pay?
drills.answer: It is recaptured. IRC § 6654(d)(2)(A)(ii) increases the next required installment determined under the flat method by the amount of the reduction, and increases later installments to the extent it has not yet been recaptured. Annualising changes when the money is due, not how much is due for the year.
drills.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

drills.prompt: A client mails a cheque to a qualified charity on 31 December. The charity deposits it on 6 January and it clears on 9 January. In which year is the contribution deductible?
drills.answer: The year of mailing. Under Reg. § 1.170A-1(b) the unconditional delivery or mailing of a cheque that subsequently clears in due course is an effective contribution on the date of delivery or mailing.
drills.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

drills.prompt: An employer tells an employee on 15 December that her bonus is available for collection any time after 20 December. She asks the employer to hold it until January and it is paid on 4 January. When is it income?
drills.answer: In the earlier year. Reg. § 1.451-2(a) treats income as constructively received when it is set apart or otherwise made available so that the taxpayer may draw on it. Her own request to defer collection is not a substantial limitation or restriction on her control.
drills.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

drills.prompt: A cash-method taxpayer pays her January mortgage instalment in December. What happens to the interest portion?
drills.answer: It is charged to capital account and treated as paid in January. IRC § 461(g)(1) applies to interest allocable to a period after the close of the taxable year in which it is paid. The points exception in § 461(g)(2) does not reach an ordinary instalment.
drills.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer files on extension in September and funds an IRA for the prior year at the same time. Is the contribution deductible for the prior year?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 219(f)(3) deems a contribution made on the last day of the preceding year only if it is made by the time prescribed by law for filing the return for that year, not including extensions.
drills.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer sells stock at a loss on 10 December, having bought additional shares of the same stock on 20 November. Is the loss allowed?
drills.answer: No, to the extent of the replacement shares. IRC § 1091(a) disallows a loss where substantially identical stock is acquired within the period beginning 30 days before the sale and ending 30 days after it. The 20 November purchase falls inside the window, and the disallowed loss is added to the basis of those shares.
drills.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer acquires stock on 2 February and sells it on 2 February of the following year. Is the gain long-term?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 1222 requires the property to be held for more than one year. The day of acquisition is excluded from the count, so the holding period first exceeds one year on 3 February. A sale on 2 February produces short-term gain.
drills.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

drills.prompt: A sole proprietor sells equipment for $48,000. Cost was $80,000 and depreciation taken was $50,000. How is the $18,000 gain characterised?
drills.answer: All ordinary income. Recomputed basis is $80,000, adjusted basis is $30,000, and IRC § 1245(a) makes ordinary the excess over adjusted basis of the lower of recomputed basis ($80,000) or amount realised ($48,000) — that is $18,000, the entire gain. Nothing is left for § 1231.
drills.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer has a net section 1231 gain of $25,000 this year and had a net section 1231 loss of $18,000 two years ago that has not been recaptured. What is the character of this year's gain?
drills.answer: $18,000 ordinary and $7,000 long-term capital. IRC § 1231(c)(1) treats net section 1231 gain as ordinary income to the extent of non-recaptured net section 1231 losses from the five most recent preceding taxable years.
drills.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

drills.prompt: A collector sells an antique held for eleven years at a $40,000 gain. Her other income puts her in the top bracket. What rate applies to the gain?
drills.answer: 28 percent. Collectibles gain is taken out of the adjusted net capital gain that receives the 0, 15 and 20 percent rates and is taxed under the separate 28-percent rate gain rule in IRC § 1(h)(4).
drills.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer acquired qualified small business stock in 2023 and sells it after four years. How much of the gain is excluded?
drills.answer: None. The stock was acquired on or before the applicable date of 4 July 2025, so it is governed by IRC § 1202(a)(1)(A), which requires a holding period of more than five years. The tiered percentages in § 1202(a)(5) apply only to stock acquired after that date.
drills.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

drills.prompt: A married couple filed separate returns for a year. Eighteen months after the due date they want to file jointly instead. May they?
drills.answer: Yes, provided none of the bars applies. IRC § 6013(b)(1) permits a joint return after separate returns, and § 6013(b)(2) closes the election only after 3 years from the unextended due date, or after a notice of deficiency has been mailed and the spouse has petitioned the Tax Court, or after a suit for recovery, closing agreement or compromise.
drills.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

drills.prompt: A married couple filed a joint return and now wish to file separately for that year. The due date has passed. May they?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 6013(b) provides only for a joint return after separate returns. There is no corresponding provision allowing the reverse after the due date, so the joint return — and the joint and several liability under § 6013(d)(3) — stands.
drills.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

drills.prompt: A married individual files a separate return. Her husband itemizes deductions. Her own itemized deductions total less than the standard deduction. What is her standard deduction?
drills.answer: Zero. IRC § 63(c)(6)(A) sets the standard deduction at zero for a married individual filing a separate return where either spouse itemizes. She must itemize whatever her own deductions come to.
drills.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

drills.prompt: A married man lived with his wife until 4 July, then moved out. His son lived with him all year and he paid the whole cost of the home. Can he be considered unmarried?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 7703(b)(3) requires the spouse not to be a member of the household during the last 6 months of the taxable year, which begins 1 July. She was a member on 1 to 4 July, so the test fails and he is married for the year.
drills.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

drills.prompt: A couple who live together file separate returns. One receives social security benefits. How much of the base amount does she get?
drills.answer: None. Under IRC § 86(c)(1)(C) the base amount is zero for a taxpayer who is married at the close of the year within the meaning of § 7703, does not file a joint return, and does not live apart from the spouse at all times during the year. The adjusted base amount is zero as well under § 86(c)(2)(C).
drills.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)
